title: From Obesity to Cancer Cachexia: PI3K/AKT/MTOR Signaling Across the Energy Balance Spectrum - A Scoping Review of Body Size, Composition, and Cancer Outcomes.
abstract: The PI3K/AKT/MTOR signaling pathway is overactivated in cancer. Obesity is an established risk factor for several cancers, also variably associated with prognosis. Cancer cachexia is at the opposite end of the energy balance spectrum and is similarly linked to poor prognosis. Preclinical studies link obesity to activation of this pathway, whereas cachexia is associated with its suppression in skeletal muscle. However, human findings are inconsistent and often ignore the metabolic influence of body composition on MTOR activity. This scoping review summarizes how body size and composition-spanning obesity to cachexia-relate to PI3K/AKT/MTOR signaling in cancer risk and outcomes. A systematic search in Web of Science, Embase, and PubMed through January 19, 2023, identified 6,285 studies; 139 met the inclusion criteria across 15 cancer types: gastrointestinal (n=48); gynecological (n=34); breast (n=30); male reproductive (n=7); lung (n=6); thyroid (n=6); renal (n=2); and skin (n=1) cancers, plus cachexia (n=5). Body size was associated with components and effectors of the PI3K/AKT/MTOR pathway, but findings were inconsistent, reflecting heterogeneity in cancer type, subtype, exposure and biomarker measurement, and unmeasured host factors. Insulin resistance and diabetes were more consistently associated with pathway markers than BMI. title: Cytolethal distending toxin promotes epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition by modulating AKT-dependent β-catenin Ser552 phosphorylation.
abstract: Bacterial genotoxins, Cytolethal Distending Toxin (CDT) and colibactin, cause DNA damage in intoxicated epithelial cells of the host. DNA damage influences β‑catenin signaling, altering its stability and nuclear translocation, potentially contributing to cancer development. Using non-transformed hepatocytes and cancer-derived intestinal and hepatic epithelial cell lines, we showed that CDT/CdtB induces the phosphorylation of β‑catenin at serine 552, along with the loss of β‑catenin from adherens junctions. This leads to the subsequent cytoplasmic accumulation and nuclear translocation of β‑catenin, ultimately driving TCF/LEF transcription, the crucial downstream event of Wnt/β‑catenin signaling, as well as the transcription of some β‑catenin target genes. Colibactin induces similar effects. MK‑2206, a direct AKT inhibitor, and metformin, a common diabetes drug that indirectly inhibits AKT, both protected cells against various effects induced by CdtB exposure. These effects include β‑catenin phosphorylation at Ser552, the disassembly of cell-cell junctions and the subsequent nuclear accumulation of phosphorylated β‑catenin, leading to enhanced TCF/LEF-mediated transcription-early molecular shifts driving the epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT). Specifically, both drugs protected against CdtB-induced EMT features, including increased nuclear accumulation of SNAIL, enhanced matrix degradation, and motility. title: Miracle and/or Minefield? GLP-1 RA Drugs and Eating Disorders.
abstract: Purpose of review Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) have transformed the treatment of obesity and type 2 diabetes (T2D), but their rapid uptake has outpaced understanding of their effects in individuals with eating disorders (EDs). GLP-1 RAs produce sustained effects on appetite, satiety, food reward, and energy intake, raising the possibility of markedly different consequences across ED presentations. Recent findings Preliminary studies suggest potential benefit for binge-eating symptoms, consistent with emerging evidence of overlap between binge eating and reward- and impulse-related pathways. Conversely, appetite suppression and attenuation of compensatory responses to negative energy balance could facilitate or mask restriction in individuals vulnerable to anorexia nervosa (AN) or atypical anorexia nervosa (AAN). Empirical evidence remains sparse. We review neurobiological and genetic evidence relevant to these potentially divergent effects, summarize the clinical literature, and highlight implications for screening and monitoring. Determining who may benefit, who may be harmed, and how to identify risk before treatment should be priorities for future research.
summary_short: Recent findings Preliminary studies suggest potential benefit for binge-eating symptoms, consistent with emerging evidence of overlap between binge eating and reward- and impulse-related pathways.

title: Rutin plus vitamin C attenuate acute doxorubicin-induced liver toxicity in rats.
abstract: Doxorubicin (DOX) is widely used to treat hepatocellular carcinoma, but its use is limited by dose-dependent hepatotoxicity associated with oxidative stress and inflammation. Protective adjunct therapies that reduce liver injury without compromising anticancer efficacy remain a clinical challenge. Here, we evaluated the hepatoprotective effects of combined rutin and vitamin C administration in a rat model of acute DOX-induced liver injury. All groups except the control received a single intraperitoneal injection of DOX (15 mg/kg) on day 12, after daily oral dosing from days 1 to 14. Animals were sacrificed on day 14 to capture the acute phase of DOX-induced hepatotoxicity, which is well documented to peak within 48-72 h after high single doses of anthracyclines. title: Effects of Anti-Diabetic Drugs on Satellite Cell Function: A Mini Review.
abstract: Metformin, glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) and sodium glucose cotransport 2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) are the most frequently prescribed medications for the treatment of diabetes. While the efficacy of these anti-diabetic drugs is clear, the underlying mechanisms of how they improve metabolism and produce other seemingly beneficial off-target effects are not clear. Several tissues including skeletal muscle have been implicated in the on-target and off-target actions of these drugs. Satellite cells are muscle stem cells that are important for skeletal muscle adaptation to stimuli such as exercise. In this mini-review, we present the emerging evidence exploring whether Metformin, GLP-1RA, SGLT2i modulate satellite cell function and if this is a relevant therapeutic target.

title: Pharmacological targeting of ageing hallmarks: molecular mechanism and clinical translation.
abstract: Background: Ageing is a gradual biological process characterized by progressive physiological decline and increased susceptibility to age-related diseases. The hallmarks of ageing provide a mechanistic framework for understanding these changes and identifying potential therapeutic targets. Objective: This review summarizes the major hallmarks of ageing, their links to age-related diseases, and pharmacological strategies targeting these mechanisms. Methods: We provide a narrative synthesis of current mechanistic and clinical evidence on candidate gerotherapeutics. Results: Pharmacological interventions targeting nutrient sensing, cellular senescence, mitochondrial dysfunction, and other aging-related pathways include metformin, rapamycin, senotherapeutics, and NAD + precursors. These agents show potential to improve healthspan and reduce disease burden, although human evidence remains heterogeneous. Conclusion: Targeting the hallmarks of ageing represents a promising therapeutic strategy, but further well-designed clinical studies are needed to establish efficacy, safety, and clinically meaningful benefits.
summary_short: Background: Ageing is a gradual biological process characterized by progressive physiological decline and increased susceptibility to age-related diseases. These agents show potential to improve healthspan and reduce disease burden, although human evidence remains heterogeneous.

title: Tafenoquine-associated serum redox metabolic remodeling during Babesia microti infection in mice.
abstract: Babesiosis is an important tick-borne parasitic disease with limited therapeutic options. Tafenoquine exhibits potent antibabesial activity, but the metabolic basis underlying its antibabesial activity remains unclear. Here, we investigated metabolic alterations associated with tafenoquine treatment during Babesia microti infection, with a focus on redox regulation. BALB/c mice infected with B. microti were treated with tafenoquine, and serum metabolites were profiled using widely targeted metabolomics. Differential metabolic changes were identified by multivariate and univariate analyses, and redox-related alterations were further evaluated together with biochemical measurements of antioxidant defense and oxidative damage markers. Serum metabolic profiles differed between tafenoquine-treated and untreated infected mice, particularly during the acute infection stage. Redox-related metabolic remodeling was characterized by alterations in metabolites involved in cysteine and methionine metabolism, glutathione metabolism, taurine and related metabolism, and the tricarboxylic acid cycle. Following tafenoquine treatment, superoxide dismutase and glutathione peroxidase activities in serum were lower, whereas malondialdehyde levels were higher, consistent with lipid peroxidation. Together, these metabolomic and biochemical findings are consistent with substantial redox metabolic remodeling associated with tafenoquine treatment during B. microti infection.

title: Markedly reduced skeletal muscle oxidative capacity with elevated circulating GDF-15 in children with cerebral palsy.
abstract: Background Cerebral palsy (CP) is associated with progressive skeletal muscle weakness and reduced physical capacity, yet the contribution of mitochondrial dysfunction to these impairments remains incompletely understood. Methods We therefore evaluated skeletal muscle mitochondrial health in children with CP and typically developing (TD) children (12.9±3.4years) using a comprehensive approach integrating high-resolution respirometry, targeted protein analyses, circulating biomarkers, and plasma proteomics. Thirty-six skeletal muscle biopsies from 22 children with CP, and 15 muscle biopsies from TD children were collected during planned orthopedic surgery. Results Skeletal muscle from children with CP exhibited markedly reduced oxidative capacity (-50% in CP vs TD, p -1 for TD vs CP, p Conclusion These findings demonstrate that previously reported reductions in skeletal muscle mitochondrial protein content in CP translate into profound impairments in mitochondrial function. Moreover, the dissociation between mitochondrial dysfunction and inflammatory signaling suggests that mitochondrial insufficiency in CP occurs independently of inflammation. Elevated circulating GDF-15 further suggests that mitochondrial dysfunction in CP may extend beyond skeletal muscle and exert systemic effects. Elevated circulating GDF-15 further suggests that mitochondrial dysfunction in CP may extend beyond skeletal muscle and exert systemic effects.

title: Does succinic acid treatment improve metabolic health in a male murine model of early ageing?
abstract: Ageing associates with obesity, mitochondrial dysfunction, and impaired glucose homeostasis. Previously, we documented that succinic acid (SA) treatment improves mitochondrial function and adiposity; however, the effects on ageing are unknown. Therefore, we determined the effect of SA treatment on metabolic health in 19 aged male mice (Age; 16 months), randomized to receive vehicle (Veh, n = 8) or SA (n = 11) and compared to young controls (Young; 6 months) (n = 24). After 6 weeks of treatment, insulin tolerance (IT), glucose tolerance (GT), pyruvate tolerance (PT) and physical activity (PA) were assessed. Body mass (BM), epididymal white adipose tissue (EWAT) and heart mass (HM) were measured at study end. Soleus muscle and EWAT underwent mitochondrial respirometry. Mice in the Age group had higher HM and EWAT (both P 0.05). PA was ∼50% lower in the Age group (8778 ± 5774 vs. 4132 ± 1523 rev/day), though Age-SA had 48% higher PA (Age-SA 6118 ± 2203 rev/day). SA treatment did not affect BM (37.8 ± 2.7 vs. 37.7 ± 3.2 g), EWAT (1.4 ± 0.4 vs. 1.3 ± 0.4 g) or HM (0.17 ± 0.01 vs. 0.19 ± 0.04 g, Age-Veh vs. Age-SA, all P > 0.05, respectively). GT AUC differed by group (P = 0.019), with Age-SA having lower AUC (Young 47120 ± 8751 vs. Age-SA 37180 ± 5383 AUC, P 0.22). SA reversed the age-associated reduction in complex I+II-driven respiration in adipose (P < 0.05). title: An approach towards standardized tissue homogenization in metabolomics for improved reproducibility, accuracy and comparability.
abstract: Introduction Tissue metabolomics enables comprehensive characterization of metabolic processes, but its application is limited by variability introduced during sample collection, storage, homogenization, extraction, and quantification. Standardization of such factors is therefore critical to ensure reproducible and comparable datasets for intra-study data processing and inter-study data merging and comparison. Objectives This study presents an optimized and standardized workflow for robust metabolite extraction from pork muscle tissue for targeted mass spectrometry, systematically evaluating key parameters affecting metabolite yield to identify conditions that maximize yield, reproducibility and metabolite class coverage. Methods The workflow integrates bead-based tissue homogenization with a two-step metabolite and lipid extraction protocol. Specifically, the impact of (i) tissue weight (TW) to homogenization solution (HS) volume ratios, (ii) different homogenate extract (HX) volumes and (iii) total homogenate volume (THV) on metabolite extraction performance is discussed. Based on metabolite class coverage, optimal conditions are identified. Results A TW-to-HS ratio of 1:12 and a HX volume of 25 µL provided better and more reproducible results. Under these standardized conditions, more than 350 metabolites were consistently quantified, spanning a wide range of chemical classes, including polar, semi-polar and non-polar species. title: Prevalent atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease is associated with osteoporosis and osteopenia in people referred for bone mineral density testing
abstract: Osteoporosis and atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) are common in older adults. This cross-sectional study examined whether ASCVD prevalence differs by bone mineral density (BMD) category in the Manitoba BMD registry ( n = 86,991 adults, mean age 64.7 ± 11.0 years, 90.2% women). Total hip (TH), femoral neck (FN), and lumbar spine (LS) BMD was assessed by dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry and categorized from T -score as normal (≥ − 1), osteopenia (− 1.0 to − 2.5), or osteoporosis (≤ − 2.5). Prevalent ASCVD (hospitalized coronary artery disease, acute myocardial infarction, non-hemorrhagic cerebrovascular disease, peripheral arterial disease; coronary revascularization; and/or congestive heart failure) was ascertained from linked data. Multivariable adjusted logistic regression assessed associations. Among individuals, 10.7% had prevalent ASCVD, 39.1% had osteopenia, and 8.6% had osteoporosis. ASCVD prevalences for the normal, osteopenia, and osteoporosis groups were 9.2%, 11.2%, and 18.2%, respectively. Compared to normal BMD, osteopenia and osteoporosis were associated with higher odds of prevalent ASCVD adjusted for fracture risk factors (OR 1.09, 95% CI 1.03–1.15; OR 1.37, 95% CI 1.27–1.49). Associations persisted with further adjustment for cardiometabolic and socioeconomic factors (osteopenia OR 1.18, 95% CI 1.12–1.25; osteoporosis OR 1.59, 95% CI 1.46–1.73). title: Sensorimotor impairment and cognitive function across the Alzheimer’s disease continuum and major depressive disorder
abstract: Sensorimotor impairments are associated with cognitive decline, but their cumulative burden across clinical subgroups is not well characterized. To test whether sensorimotor burden is associated with baseline cognition and modifies subgroup-related cognitive differences. We analyzed 511 community-dwelling older adults. Participants were classified as cognitively normal, preclinical Alzheimer’s disease (Clinical Dementia Rating score of 0 with amyloid positron-emission tomography positivity), mild cognitive impairment, or major depressive disorder. Cognition was measured with the Preclinical Alzheimer Cognitive Composite. A Sensorimotor Index summed impairments in grip strength, gait speed, reaction time, hearing, vision, and olfaction and was categorized as low (0–1) or elevated (≥ 2). Multivariable linear regression assessed subgroup, index, and subgroup-by-index terms, adjusting for age, sex, race, education, apolipoprotein E ε4 status, and neighborhood deprivation. Without interactions, elevated burden was associated with lower cognitive scores (β =− 0.374; 95% confidence interval, − 0.508 to − 0.240; p < 0.001). In the interaction model, the mild cognitive impairment-by-elevated-index (β =− 0.647; 95% confidence interval, − 0.981 to − 0.313; p < 0.001) and major depressive disorder-by-elevated-index terms (β =− 0.440; 95% confidence interval, − 0.759 to − 0.120; p = 0.007) were significant; the preclinical Alzheimer’s disease interaction was not. title: Epigenetic clock choice matters: systematic variation in age estimation and socioeconomic patterning of biological aging
abstract: Epigenetic clocks based on DNA methylation (DNAm) are common tools in aging research. While first-generation clocks were developed to predict chronological age, second- and third-generation clocks aim to capture aspects of biological aging. However, little is known about how different clocks compare in estimating deviations between chronological and DNAm age and their sensitivity to social and life stage disparities in population-based samples. This study examines delta age across epigenetic clocks from three generations (1st-Horvath, 2nd-PhenoAge, 3rd-DunedinPoAm), focusing on estimation patterns and socioeconomic gradients. Data stem from the UK Household Longitudinal Study, including DNAm profiles and socioeconomic measures. Delta age was computed as the difference between DNAm and chronological age. Linear mixed-effects models assessed delta age by clock type, age group, sex, and interactions with socioeconomic status (education, occupation, income), adjusting for batch effects and cell composition. Substantial variation in delta age emerged across clocks and age groups. First-generation clocks overestimated age in younger and underestimated it in older individuals. The second-generation clock showed consistent negative delta age. The third-generation clock displayed minimal deviation and stable calibration. title: Dietary nucleotides and NAD+ precursors in age-related sarcopenia
abstract: Sarcopenia is a progressive, age-related skeletal muscle disorder characterised by reduced muscle strength, accompanied by loss of muscle mass and impaired muscle function. Growing interest in nutrition in older adults has also increased attention to nucleotides as potentially relevant dietary components that may participate in muscle regeneration, energy metabolism, and cellular responses to stress. The aim of this review was to critically evaluate evidence on conventional dietary nucleotides, nucleoproteins, and compounds related to NAD+ metabolism in the context of muscle ageing and sarcopenia. A structured literature review was conducted, with study identification and selection carried out in accordance with selected elements of PRISMA 2020. A total of 3090 records were identified in PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and the Web of Science Core Collection. After removal of 1327 duplicates, 1763 unique records were screened. Of 159 publications assessed in full text, 62 were retained. Three additional clinical reports identified during revision brought the qualitative synthesis to 65 publications. The most direct evidence for conventional nucleotides comes from cellular and animal models and from several human intervention studies. These findings indicate the potential to attenuate atrophy, support myogenesis, and improve selected functional outcomes. title: The human microbiome in non-communicable diseases: Mechanistic insights into dysbiosis, systemic inflammation, and precision therapeutics.
abstract: The human microbiome contributes to immune regulation, metabolic homeostasis, epithelial barrier integrity, and inter-organ communication. This review integrates evidence from gut, oral, skin, and cervicovaginal microbiomes, focusing on epithelial barrier dysfunction, altered microbial metabolite signaling, innate immune activation, inflammatory signaling, immune dysregulation, and host-microbe interactions across non-communicable diseases and microbiome-based therapeutic approaches in these contexts. Collectively, current evidence suggests that dysbiosis may represent not only a disease-associated microbial signature but also a potential mechanistic contributor to disease development and progression, although substantial interindividual and disease-specific variability remains. Microbiome-based diagnostics, fecal microbiota transplantation, personalized nutrition, and microbial therapeutics show considerable translational potential; nevertheless, causal relationships and clinical efficacy remain insufficiently established for several applications. Future research should therefore prioritize rigorously designed interventional and longitudinal studies integrating multi-omics profiling with host genetics and immune phenotyping to establish causal mechanisms, identify reproducible biomarkers, and support the development of precision microbiome-based therapeutic strategies.

title: Engineering the β-cell microenvironment: a critical strategy for insulin-producing cell survival and therapeutic applications.
abstract: Insulin-producing cells (IPCs) generated from human pluripotent stem cells (hPSCs) are a promising cell source for β-cell replacement therapy in patients with diabetes. Despite substantial advances, optimizing IPC differentiation efficiency and maturation, as well as long-term functional stability after transplantation, remains challenging. One strategy to enhance IPC function and survival is to utilize native extracellular matrix (ECM) components present within the pancreatic islet niche. ECM components activate intracellular signaling pathways essential for cell adhesion, survival, and insulin gene expression. Researchers have developed various scaffolds to reconstitute these components in vitro . This review integrates current insights into ECM-IPC interactions, focusing on scaffold composition, physical properties, and bioactive modifications that enhance IPC viability and function and discusses how these scaffold properties could improve the outcomes of β-cell replacement therapy in diabetes.

title: Sirolimus is associated with longer relapse-free survival than cyclosporine in autoimmune hemolytic anemia and evans syndrome: a retrospective cohort study.
abstract: This single-center retrospective cohort study compared sirolimus plus glucocorticoids with cyclosporine plus glucocorticoids in 37 and 35 patients with autoimmune hemolytic anemia/Evans syndrome, evaluating treatment response, long-term relapse, and exploratory patient-reported outcomes (PROs). Response and relapse were assessed longitudinally, and relapse-free survival was analyzed using time-to-event methods. PRO data (SF-36/HADS/FACIT) were available only for subsets of the sirolimus cohort and were not collected in the cyclosporine group. No statistically significant differences in overall or complete response rates were detected between the sirolimus (78.4% and 47.3%) and cyclosporine (80.0% and 52.8%) groups ( P > 0.05). Median relapse-free survival was not reached in the sirolimus group versus 1455 days in the cyclosporine group ( P P < 0.05). These findings are hypothesis-generating given the nonrandomized design, small heterogeneous cohort, baseline imbalances, and incomplete drug-level monitoring, and require confirmation in prospective studies.

title: Effect of 5-Aminolevulinic Acid on the Proliferation of Sheep Rumen Epithelial Cells.
abstract: Objective The rumen plays a central role in digestion and metabolism in ruminants, and rumen epithelial cell proliferation is important for rumen development in lambs. However, the regulatory effects of 5-aminolevulinic acid (5-ALA) on this process remain unclear. This study aimed to investigate the effects of 5-ALA on the proliferation of primary rumen epithelial cells isolated from lambs and elucidate the underlying regulatory mechanisms. Methods Primary rumen epithelial cells were isolated and cultured, and different concentrations of 5-ALA were applied to the treatment groups. Rapamycin (RAPA), an inhibitor of mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1), was used to assess the involvement of mTORC1 in the responses to 5-ALA. In addition, cell viability, proliferation, DNA synthesis, mitochondrial membrane potential, ATP content, and the expression of PI3K/Akt/mTOR pathway-related proteins and cell-cycle regulatory proteins were measured. title: Tramadol potentiates chemotherapy efficacy in hepatocellular carcinoma cells.
abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is the sixth most common cancer and the third leading cause of cancer-related deaths, leading to poor responses to chemotherapy. Cancer-related pain affects up to 90% of these patients, significantly impairing their quality of life. Tramadol, a prescribed analgesic for cancer pain, has shown anti-tumour effects in various malignancies, yet its potential in HCC remains largely unexplored. In this study, we investigated tramadol's anti-proliferative, pro-apoptotic, and autophagy-inducing effects in HepG2, Hep3B, and Huh7 cell lines. Tramadol significantly inhibits cell proliferation in a dose-dependent manner, leading to a reduction in the S-phase and subG1 phase accumulation. It induces apoptosis in HepG2 and Hep3B, increases late apoptosis/necrosis, and enhances autophagy. Additionally, tramadol increased the cytotoxicity of cisplatin and 5-fluorouracil, with significant reductions in their IC50 values. Overall, tramadol inhibits HCC growth, promotes apoptosis, and enhances chemotherapy efficacy, suggesting it could be a dual-benefit therapeutic strategy for HCC.
summary_short: Additionally, tramadol increased the cytotoxicity of cisplatin and 5-fluorouracil, with significant reductions in their IC50 values.

title: Werner Syndrome With Multisystem Manifestations in a 35-Year-Old Bangladeshi Man: A Case Report.
abstract: Werner syndrome, also known as adult progeria, is a rare autosomal recessive disorder characterized by premature aging and multisystem involvement. We report the case of a 35-year-old Bangladeshi man who presented with growth arrest during adolescence resulting in short stature, bilateral posterior subcapsular cataracts, diabetes mellitus, hypothyroidism, chronic non-healing ulcers, scleroderma-like skin changes, muscle wasting, and ankle ankylosis. Molecular genetic analysis identified a pathogenic WRN gene variant (c.3233 + 2 T >C in intron 26), confirming the diagnosis of Werner syndrome. A younger sister exhibited similar phenotypic features, suggesting possible familial occurrence; however, she was not genetically tested. Laboratory investigations revealed normocytic normochromic anemia, hypertriglyceridemia, elevated gonadotropin levels, markedly reduced serum testosterone, and marked hyperferritinemia. In addition, radiological evaluation demonstrated generalized osteopenia with talocalcaneal and ankle joint ankylosis, while electrocardiography revealed left ventricular hypertrophy. Management focused on long-term control of metabolic and endocrine comorbidities together with comprehensive wound care for chronic ulcers. This case highlights the importance of early recognition, molecular confirmation, multidisciplinary management, and regular surveillance for cardiovascular complications and malignancies in patients with Werner syndrome.

abstract: Background Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a demyelinating disease of the central nervous system (CNS). Changes in the microenvironment surrounding oligodendrocyte progenitor cells (OPCs), characterized by excessive production of extracellular matrix (ECM) components driven by elevated TGF-β and CTGF signaling, impair the remyelination capacity of these cells. Decorin (DCN), an endogenous inhibitor of the TGF-β/CTGF signaling axis, has emerged as a potential regulator of ECM homeostasis. Remyelination and oligodendroglial lineage dynamics were assessed using Luxol Fast Blue (LFB) staining and analysis of MBP and NG2 expression. title: FDG PET Biodistribution Patterns of Patients on GLP-1 Therapies.
abstract: Purpose The use of glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) therapies continues to increase, but there is limited literature on their effect on fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) biodistribution and minimal society guidelines. This study presents observations on a cohort of findings associated with GLP-1 use among patients undergoing oncologic FDG PET/CT, with attention to factors that may complicate image interpretation. Materials and methods This retrospective observational study included 116 adult patients from a single academic center who reported use of a GLP-1. Medical information and demographic information were compiled, and images were analyzed for abnormal biodistribution. Statistical analysis was performed to determine association between these factors and atypical uptake. Results This study found areas of altered FDG biodistribution in 75.9% (88/116) of patients with uptake noted in the esophagus, small intestines, large intestines, and muscles. Muscle uptake was seen in 21.6% of patients including one patient whose scan was considered nondiagnostic. There was no significant association between muscle uptake and age, sex, BMI, time since last GLP-1 dose, NPO time, blood glucose level, individual GLP-1 medications, insulin usage, metformin usage, other antidiabetic drug usage, systemic steroid usage, or GI symptoms. title: Real-World Initiation of Resmetirom and Recorded Incretin Exposure in the United States.
abstract: Aims Resmetirom and semaglutide 2.4 mg are approved for metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis but have not been tested together. We examined recorded incretin exposure among resmetirom initiators and the frequency and correlates of co-initiation. Materials and methods This new-user cohort study used TriNetX US Collaborative Network health records of patients first prescribed resmetirom from 14 March 2024 to 16 July 2026. Results Of 6837 initiators, 76.6% had overweight/obesity (code or body mass index [BMI] ≥ 30 kg/m 2 ), 44.0% Type 2 diabetes and 16.8% a cirrhosis code. An incretin prescription was recorded in 37.2%, mostly before resmetirom (33.8%; excluded from the comparison). Of the remaining 4524, 231 (5.1%) were co-initiators. Coded overweight/obesity (49.4% vs. 49.0%; SMD: 0.01) and Type 2 diabetes (30.3% vs. 33.1%; SMD: 0.06) were similar; co-initiation was about 5% in every stratum (Mantel-Haenszel odds ratios: overweight/obesity 1.08 [95% CI: 0.80-1.46]; diabetes 1.00 [0.75-1.34]). Redirecting sulfur metabolic flux by Fe(II) in a simulated composting system: From H<sub>2</sub>S emission to oxidative immobilization.
abstract: Hydrogen sulfide (H 2 S) from food waste composting is a major odor pollutant. This study investigated H 2 S source reduction via iron regulated sulfur metabolism during food waste composting. Using a quartz-sand simulation system, two Fe(II) (ferrous chloride) concentrations (0.05%, 0.5%) were tested. In the blank control (CK), H 2 S peaked at 812 mg/m 3 , cumulatively emitting 2454 mg/m 3 over 21 days. The optimal 0.5% Fe(II) completely suppressed H 2 S emission. Mechanistically, Fe(II) precipitated sulfide as FeS (partially converted to pyrite, 8.81 mg/kg) and may form a microbially mediated Fe(II) regeneration cycle, enabling continuous sulfide immobilization without inhibiting microbial activity. Functional gene analysis revealed that 0.5% Fe(II) suppressed dissimilatory sulfate reduction genes Sat and Apr (peaks falling to 47.3% and 27.3% of CK), reducing sulfide ion content by 94.5%. Conversely, sulfide oxidation gene Sqr was upregulated 212.4%-258.3% (days 3-5), shifting sulfur metabolic flux from reduction to oxidation. Metabolomics identified 210 differential metabolites, with reduced intermediates downregulated (e.g., bisulfite, thiosulfate) and oxidized/stable compounds upregulated, with significant enrichment in cysteine/methionine, sulfur, and taurine metabolism. In conclusion, 0.5% Fe(II) efficiently reduced H 2 S by redirecting sulfur flux toward oxidative immobilization, establishing a benign Fe(II) cycle.

title: All-Trans Retinoic Acid (ATRA) Attenuates Alcoholic Steatohepatitis (ASH) via reprogramming hepatic lipid metabolism in male mice.
abstract: Alcoholic steatohepatitis (ASH) is characterized by hepatic lipid accumulation, oxidative and endoplasmic reticulum stress, inflammation, and impaired autophagy, yet pharmacological options remain limited. All-trans retinoic acid (ATRA), the transcriptionally active metabolite of vitamin A, regulates retinoid receptor-dependent metabolic and stress-response pathways. We investigated whether ATRA protects against ethanol-induced liver injury in male C57BL/6 N mice fed a control Lieber-DeCarli diet, an ethanol-containing Lieber-DeCarli diet, or the ethanol diet plus ATRA (15 mg/kg, oral gavage, three times weekly). ATRA reduced hepatic triglyceride accumulation, serum alanine aminotransferase activity, and histological steatosis. These protective effects were associated with downregulation of the lipogenic and ethanol-metabolizing genes together with increased Rxra expression. title: Combining metabolomics and genomics to describe genetic factors affecting the metabolism in growing Duroc pigs.
abstract: Background Metabolites are molecular phenotypes that can provide insights into the basic biological mechanisms underlying complex phenotypes. In this study, we combined high-throughput untargeted plasma metabolomics, analysing over 700 metabolites (including lipids, amino acids, nucleotides, peptides, carbohydrates, cofactors and vitamins, partially characterised molecules, energy-related metabolites and uncharacterised metabolites) and genomic data in a population of growing purebred Duroc pigs. Through this approach, we identified genetically influenced metabolites (GIM), metabolite Quantitative Trait Loci (mQTL) and candidate genes that control metabolite levels and key metabolic pathways. mQTL were detected from metabolite genome-wide association studies (mGWAS) for single metabolites and their ratios, as well as by integrating results from conditional mGWAS. Results Genomic heritability (h² G ) of 354 metabolites (~ 60% of the filtered metabolomic dataset) was ≥ 0.10, with gamma-glutamylglycine having the highest value (h² G = 0.83). In total, 71 mQTL regions were identified, encompassing 162 metabolites (101 from single metabolite GWAS and 61 from metabolite ratio GWAS). Across all associations, individual SNP explained an average of 15.34 ± 8.38% of the phenotypic variance, with values ranging from 8.12% for N-formylmethionine to 43.50% for N6-methyllysine, which also exhibited the strongest association (p-value = 8.98 × 10 - 36 ). title: Meconopsis bhutanica alleviates liver fibrosis mediated by PPARγ activation.
abstract: Meconopsis bhutanica Tosh.Yoshida & Grey-Wilson, recorded in Tibetan Medical Book such as "Yuewang Yaozhen" and "Jingzhu Bencao", are renowned for their therapeutic properties, including heat clearing, cough-relieving, pain-alleviating, and bruise-treating effects. However, information regarding this species remains limited, and its hepatoprotective activity has yet to be reported. This study aimed to evaluate the anti-fibrotic effects of M. bhutanica extract (MBE) on liver fibrosis, characterized its major constituents, and elucidated its mechanisms using multi-omics and computational analyses. Flavonoids and phenylethanoid glycosides were identified as major constituents of MBE. MBE treatment significantly reduced serum AST, ALT, and ALP, enhanced antioxidant enzyme activity, and decreased MDA and pro-inflammatory cytokines. It suppressed collagen deposition, attenuated lipid accumulation, and regulated taurine and hypotaurine metabolism. Multi-omics analyses revealed activation of peroxisome proliferators-activated receptors γ (PPARγ) and inhibition of mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) signaling. Single-cell transcriptomics confirmed reduced PPARγ activity in collagen-producing hepatic stellate cells from human cirrhotic livers. title: Microbial bile acid deconjugation counters metabolic decline in aging.
abstract: Interventions such as caloric restriction and time-restricted feeding improve lifespan and aging-associated metabolic health, in part through effects on the gut microbiome and bile acid dynamics. However, how aging alters microbial function and bile acid signaling, and whether these changes can be therapeutically leveraged, remain unclear. Here, we show that aged mice exhibit increased deconjugation of taurine-conjugated bile acids accompanied by increased bile salt hydrolase (BSH)-related transcriptional activity. Individuals with exceptional longevity show a similar bile acid deconjugation signature, suggesting an association with resilient or exceptional aging. Using engineered native bacteria, we further increased luminal BSH activity in aged mice and improved insulin sensitivity, accompanied by supportive changes in body composition and other metabolic readouts. Together, these findings suggest that elevated BSH activity may have a protective role during aging. They challenge the view that age-related changes in bile acid biotransformations are uniformly detrimental, highlighting microbial bile acid modulation as a potential strategy to improve late-life metabolic health.

title: Taurine metabolism: a potential target for neuroprotection in age-related neurodegenerative diseases.
abstract: Taurine is one of the most abundant free amino acids in mammals and plays essential roles in cellular homeostasis, mitochondrial function, calcium regulation and neuronal survival. Taurine availability varies markedly across tissues, species and sexes, reflecting the balance between endogenous synthesis, dietary intake, transport and efflux. Although reduced taurine levels have been reported in some aging tissues, recent longitudinal studies indicate that circulating taurine does not decline universally with age, and its value as a biomarker of aging remains debated. Alterations in taurine or its transporter SLC6A6 have been described in Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, multiple sclerosis, Huntington's disease and retinal degenerations. Preclinical studies indicate that taurine supplementation mitigates excitotoxicity, stabilizes mitochondrial function, reduces neuroinflammation and supports myelination and synaptic balance. Despite this strong mechanistic rationale, clinical evidence remains limited and heterogeneous, underscoring the need for biomarker-guided trials and a clearer definition of optimal therapeutic windows. In this review, we summarize the general properties of taurine and its metabolic regulation. title: Linking the fine structural characteristics of cereal β-glucans to their differential protective effects against colitis.
abstract: Although cereal β-glucans exert protective effects against experimental colitis, the relationship between their fine structural and physicochemical properties and differential in vivo responses remains unclear. This study directly compared highland barley β-glucan (BBG) and oat β-glucan (OBG), two high-purity mixed-linkage β-(1 → 3)/(1 → 4)-D-glucans, under identical experimental conditions. BBG had a higher cellotriosyl-to-cellotetraosyl (DP3/DP4) ratio than OBG (2.33 vs. 1.51) and a lower weight-average molecular weight. In dextran sulfate sodium (DSS)-induced colitis mice, both β-glucans alleviated clinical signs of disease, while BBG showed greater protection at the tissue and biochemical levels. BBG preserved colon length at 4.88 cm, compared with 4.46 cm for OBG. It reduced myeloperoxidase activity, nitric oxide, and malondialdehyde levels to 1226 U g -1 , 0.42 μmol g -1 , and 78.8 nmol mg -1 , respectively, and fully restored Claudin-1 expression. BBG was also associated with enrichment of Ligilactobacillus , Limosilactobacillus , Romboutsia , and Turicibacter and suppression of Escherichia-Shigella . Fecal metabolomics showed higher levels of selected indole derivatives and taurine-conjugated bile acids, accompanied by lower uric acid and prostaglandin-related inflammatory metabolites. title: Ocular Safety of GLP-1 Receptor Agonists: A Comprehensive Review.
abstract: Background Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) provide substantial glycemic and cardiometabolic benefits, but concerns regarding diabetic retinopathy (DR) progression and nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION) have raised questions about their ocular safety. This review critically evaluates current evidence and its clinical implications. Methods A structured literature search of PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, and Scopus was conducted from inception through July 2026. Evidence from randomized trials, observational studies, meta-analyses, pharmacovigilance investigations, clinical guidelines, and regulatory documents was narratively synthesized. Results In SUSTAIN-6, semaglutide increased DR complications compared with placebo (3.0% vs. 1.8%; hazard ratio 1.76, 95% confidence interval 1.11-2.78), predominantly among patients with pre-existing retinopathy and substantial early glycemic improvement. However, subsequent trials and meta-analyses did not establish a consistent class-wide increase in retinopathy risk. Early worsening appears more closely associated with rapid glycemic reduction than with established direct retinal toxicity. Observational and pharmacovigilance studies have identified a potential association between GLP-1 RAs and NAION, although conflicting findings, limited event numbers, and residual confounding preclude definitive causal inference. title: Surface-engineered Mo<sub>2</sub>B<sub>2</sub> MBene for controlled 5-fluorouracil delivery: A DFT insight into adsorption and electronic mechanisms.
abstract: Density functional theory (DFT) calculations were performed to evaluate pristine and functionalized MBene Mo 2 B 2 (F, O, S, H) as nanocarriers for anticancer drugs 5-fluorouracil (5Flu) and metformin (Met). Surface functionalization significantly modulates structural stability, electronic properties, and drug-surface interactions. Among all systems, O-functionalization exhibits the highest stability and strongest electronic tuning. Adsorption analysis shows that 5Flu displays moderate and tunable binding, with Mo 2 B 2 -O achieving near-optimal adsorption energy, ensuring a balance between drug loading and controlled release. In contrast, Met exhibits excessively strong chemisorption on all surfaces, limiting its release capability. Electronic (HOMO-LUMO, DOS) and NBO analyses reveal enhanced charge transfer and orbital hybridization in O-functionalized systems, while NCI results indicate van der Waals-dominated interactions for 5Flu and stronger donor-acceptor interactions for Met. Optical analysis demonstrates tunable absorption and enhanced charge-transfer characteristics upon functionalization. Overall, Mo 2 B 2 -O emerges as a promising platform for efficient and controlled 5Flu delivery in cancer therapy.

title: Indole-3-propionic acid attenuates O-GlcNAc-associated oxidative stress and DNA damage responses to preserve intestinal stem cell homeostasis.
abstract: Intestinal stem cell (ISC) homeostasis progressively declines during aging, leading to impaired intestinal renewal and dysfunction. Aberrant O- linked β-N-acetylglucosamine ( O- GlcNAc) modification and persistent DNA damage response (DDR) activation are emerging as key causes of aging and age-related diseases. Indole-3-propionic acid (IPA), a tryptophan metabolite produced by the gut microbiota, exhibits antioxidant and cytoprotective activities; however, its role in age-associated ISC dysfunction has not been defined. In this study, we examined the effects of IPA in Drosophila models of physiological aging, pharmacological O- GlcNAc elevation, and genetic OGA depletion. IPA suppressed ISC hyperproliferation while attenuating DDR activation, as evidenced by reduced γH2AVD and pS/TQ levels in aged and Thiamet G-treated flies. In parallel, IPA decreased excessive O- GlcNAcylation and intracellular reactive oxygen species (ROS) accumulation under both conditions. To assess whether these protective effects were mediated through O- GlcNAc signaling, we evaluated OGA knockdown flies and found that IPA effectively rescued OGA depletion-induced ISC hyperproliferation, excessive O- GlcNAcylation, ROS accumulation, and DDR activation. At the tissue level, IPA improved intestinal morphology and restored epithelial barrier function. abstract: Background Population aging in Nigeria underscores the need for healthy longevity medicine (HLM), yet little is known about how religious affiliation is associated with perceptions of and interest in HLM services. Objective To assess the association of religion and age with Nigerians' perceptions of and interest in HLM. Methods An online cross-sectional survey was conducted among Nigerian adults using convenience and snowball sampling through social media. title: Tailoring metal-organic framework catalysts for exchange reactions within covalent adaptable networks.
abstract: Catalyst immobilisation offers a route to controlling bond exchange in covalent adaptable networks (CANs), yet the interplay between base identity, catalytic activity and network properties remains insufficiently understood. Here, we expand a heterogeneous catalytic platform by immobilising three organic bases-4-dimethylaminopyridine (DMAP), 1,1,3,3-tetramethylguanidine (TMG) and 1,5,7-triazabicyclo[4.4.0]dec-5-ene (TBD)-on a zirconium-based metal-organic framework called UiO-66. Their comparison in dynamic photopolymer networks reveals distinct effects of immobilisation on thiol-thioester exchange. UiO-DMAP and UiO-TMG exhibit lower catalytic activity than their free-base counterparts, consistent with partial restriction of accessibility, nucleophilicity and basicity. In contrast, UiO-TBD retains its catalytic activity, demonstrating that the consequences of immobilisation depend critically on base structure. Beyond exchange kinetics, the immobilised bases influence the mechanical properties of the resulting CANs. Only UiO-TMG exhibits the smallest nanocrystalline domain, as evidenced by small-angle X-ray diffraction, and its incorporation yields networks with enhanced Young's modulus and toughness, suggesting a contribution of MOF crystalline domain to mechanical reinforcement. title: Metabolic syndrome and Alzheimer's disease: Mechanistic links and precision prevention (Review).
abstract: Metabolic syndrome (MetS) is associated with increased risk of Alzheimer's disease (AD), however, the majority of previous studies regard MetS as an isolated risk factor and focus on single pathways, lacking systematic understanding of combined effects among multiple metabolic components. The present review systematically summarizes the multifaceted mechanisms by which MetS promotes AD pathology, including insulin resistance and cerebral energy dysregulation, oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction, neuroinflammation and glial cell activation, vascular dysfunction and dysregulation of the renin‑angiotensin system, as well as the central convergent signaling pathway involving glycogen synthase kinase‑3β. The present review further highlights emerging regulatory mechanisms involving the gut‑brain axis, epigenetic reprogramming, sex differences and hormonal effects and senescent microenvironment. By emphasizing the peripheral‑central crosstalk and interactive amplification of MetS components, the present review aimed to position AD as a central manifestation of systemic metabolic disorders in the brain and propose a multi‑domain precision strategy integrating lifestyle intervention, metabolic drug repurposing, gut microbiota regulation, anti‑aging therapy and biomarker‑guided subtype classification for intervention against MetS‑associated AD.

abstract: The number of reproductive-aged solid organ transplant recipients continues to rise, underscoring the need for comprehensive reproductive health counseling that spans throughout the transplant continuum. Fertility is often impaired in end-stage organ disease but often resumes within months after transplantation, which may cause unintended pregnancy during a period of heightened maternal, fetal, and allograft vulnerability. This review synthesizes the evidence and expert consensus from the American Society of Transplantation Women's Health Community of Practice Controversies Conference on contraception, infertility, and immunosuppression in reproductive-aged female transplant recipients. Recommendations are largely US-based, although reference to international variability is noted, where relevant. We outline contraceptive options with attention to efficacy and safety in transplant recipients. Data on infertility and assisted reproductive technologies in solid organ transplant recipients remain limited, although emerging evidence supports the feasibility and safety of ovulation induction, in vitro fertilization, and single-embryo transfer with careful monitoring for complications such as ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome. title: Metabolomics and lipidomics in the differentiation of CIN 2 and CIN 3: an exploratory pilot study.
abstract: Introduction High-grade cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN 2-3) is a precursor lesion to cervical cancer and, although it presents different probabilities of regression and progression, it is usually grouped together in screening and managed similarly. However, the mechanisms that determine its evolution are still poorly understood, and standard treatment by conization can lead to reproductive complications such as subfertility and premature birth. Objective This study aimed to identify metabolic and lipid signatures that can distinguish between CIN 2 and CIN 3 lesions using liquid chromatography-high-resolution mass spectrometry (LC-HRMS). Methods Tissue samples from the lesion and adjacent margin of 24 women with CIN 2-3 were subjected to metabolomic and lipidomic analysis by LC-HRMS. Multivariate statistical analyses, pathway analysis, and correlation were performed to understand these neoplasms' development and progression and identify potential metabolites and lipids to distinguish such lesions. Results Metabolomic and lipidomic analysis by LC-HRMS in cervical tissue identified molecular signatures with differential abundance between CIN 2 and CIN 3, highlighting patterns associated with the degree of lesion. Multivariate analyses highlighted metabolites (serine, glutamic acid, guanidine-6-monophosphate, succinic acid, mannose 6-phosphate, and taurine) and lipids (TG 49:1, TG 50:1, and TG 52:2) as the main contributors to the discrimination between the groups, sugge

title: Elevated malonic acid and 15d-PGJ2 in MASLD rats with diabetes triggered pathological cardiac remodeling through impairment of mitochondrial health and cellular metabolism.
abstract: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) significantly raises the risk of cardiovascular disease (CVD) and makes it the leading cause of death in affected individuals. Despite growing evidence, the liver-heart connection remains poorly understood. MASLD was induced in male SD rats using an 8-week high-fat diet along with a single streptozotocin dose at week 6. Cardiac changes were assessed by echocardiography, electrocardiography, and histopathology. Two altered metabolites identified by LC-MS/MS were evaluated in cardiomyoblasts (MTT, JC-1, MitoSOX, & Seahorse) and in rats to assess cardiac structure and function. MASLD rats with diabetes exhibited increased LV mass, wall thickness, diastolic diameter, and volume, with reduced ejection fraction, fractional shortening, cardiac output, and stroke volume. Histology confirmed cardiomyocyte hypertrophy, fibrosis, and hepatic lipid accumulation. LC-MS/MS identified elevated malonic acid and 15-deoxy-12,14-prostaglandin J2 (15d-PGJ2) in serum. In cardiomyoblasts, these metabolites increased mitochondrial ROS, reduced membrane potential, and decreased metabolites such as taurine, arginine, succinate, and l-glutamine. Eight weeks of in vivo treatment with malonic acid and 15d-PGJ2 induced pathological cardiac remodeling, fibrosis, and subendocardial ischemia. title: Identification of gamma-hydroxybutyrate (GHB)-β-ribose as a promising biomarker enabling prolonged detection of GHB intake.
abstract: For several years, forensic toxicologists have sought biomarkers to extend the detection window of gamma-hydroxybutyric acid (GHB), a drug suspected to be involved in drug-facilitated sexual assaults yet difficult to detect due to its rapid elimination, endogenous presence, and postsampling formation. In this study, we used samples from 30 participants in a double-blind, controlled trial, randomized to placebo or a single oral dose (50 milligrams per kilogram) of sodium oxybate, a GHB salt. We collected whole blood and urine samples over 5 days and used untargeted metabolomics to search for biomarkers. The most promising feature, previously suggested as a GHB-pentose, was identified as GHB-β-ribose by chemical synthesis and liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry. Quantification showed elevated levels of GHB-β-ribose for up to 48 in blood and 24 hours in urine after GHB intake compared with endogenous levels in the placebo group and authentic forensic cases. Thus, we present GHB-β-ribose as a very promising biomarker for GHB intake, with the potential to extend the detection window for GHB.

title: Acarbose ameliorates age-related spatial learning and memory deficits in a mouse model of normal aging but not Alzheimer's disease
abstract: Introduction Declines in function occur in both “normal” aging (in the absence of disease) and age-related pathological contexts, like Alzheimer’s disease (AD). Whether “anti-aging” interventions (that extend lifespan) also promote cognitive function in aging and AD remains largely unexplored. Methods We assessed the effect of acarbose (1000 ppm from 4 months of age) on spatial learning and memory using the Morris water maze in young adult (6 mo), mid-aged (12 mo), or aged (24 mo) cohorts of normal aging (Ntg-HET3) and AD-relevant (5xFAD-HET3) genetically heterogeneous mice. Results In middle-aged and aged Ntg-HET3 mice, acarbose (ACA) treatment moderately improved age-related deficits in spatial learning and robustly ameliorated impairments in spatial memory, maintaining performance at levels equivalent to young adults, with a progressively greater effect at older ages. Conversely, ACA failed to improve progressively worsening AD-related cognitive impairments in 5xFAD-HET3 mice. Discussion This work demonstrates that anti-aging interventions can also promote cognitive longevity in normal aging. Further, it highlights that AD does not simply reflect an accelerated aging process and requires therapies beyond anti-aging interventions that target its unique molecular and cellular drivers. title: Efficacy and Safety of Biosimilar Insulin Aspart (Rapilin®) Versus Originator (NovoRapid®) in Type 1 Diabetes: A Multicenter, Retrospective Cohort Study.
abstract: Introduction Data on the biosimilar insulin aspart Rapilin® ("Biosimilar") in patients with T1DM, particularly in children and adolescents, remain scarce. This study compared the real-world efficacy and safety of Biosimilar and the originator insulin aspart NovoRapid® ("Originator") in patients with type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM). Methods Electronic medical records from 34 hospitals in China covering the period from January 1, 2023 to January 31, 2026 served as the data source for this multicenter, retrospective cohort study. A total of 229 patients with T1DM who had been receiving continuous Biosimilar (n = 116) or Originator (n = 113) treatment for ≥ 12 weeks were included. The primary endpoint was the change in glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) from baseline to the last measurement before January 31, 2026. Treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs) were collected and classified. Results Of the 229 included patients, 112 (48.9%) were men. title: Enhancing bone defect repair by core-shell nanofibrous scaffolds through phase separation-activated autophagy process along with neurogenesis.
abstract: Bone defects caused by aging or trauma often involve sensory loss, highlighting the need for scaffolds that support both bone regeneration and sensory recovery. This study reports an amino-modified mesoporous bioactive glass (MBG-NH 2 )/K63@silk fibroin (SF)/nerve growth factor (NGF) nanofiber scaffold. The scaffold showed nanoscale porosity, favorable mechanical properties, and calcium deposition in R-simulated body fluid (R-SBF). It promoted osteogenic differentiation of bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells (BMSCs) through Erk1/2-Runx2 signaling and induced autophagy via K63/p62/LC3-mediated separation, accompanied by increased expression of osteogenesis- and neurogenesis-specific genes. The scaffold supported neural differentiation, as indicated by increased expression of neurogenesis-related genes. The MBG-NH 2 /K63@SF/NGF scaffold significantly improved skull bone repair and the formation of new neurons within Haversian canals in the defect area of mice. The MBG-NH 2 /K63@SF/NGF scaffold promotes autophagy through phase separation and facilitates bone regeneration and neuron formation, indicating its potential as a multifunctional biomaterial for bone defect repair with neuron formation.
summary_short: The scaffold supported neural differentiation, as indicated by increased expression of neurogenesis-related genes. The MBG-NH 2 /K63@SF/NGF scaffold significantly improved skull bone repair and the formation of new neurons within Haversian canals in the defect area of mice.

title: Astrocytes contribute to long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acid metabolism affecting microglia in fragile X syndrome.
abstract: Polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) influence membrane structure and function, energy metabolism, inflammation, and the ability to regulate microglial activity. We show involvement of astrocytes in long-chain PUFA metabolism in human induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC)-derived astrocytes with fragile X syndrome (FXS). FXS astrocytes secreted more n-6 docosapentaenoic acid (n-6 DPA) and displayed a higher n-3 DPA to docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) ratio in medium than controls, consistent with an altered n-6 to n-3 PUFA balance in plasma from the FXS mouse. The FXS-specific increase in n-6 DPA secretion was abolished by treatment with all- trans retinoic acid (ATRA), which affected gene expression in astrocyte subpopulations and modulated secreted triacylglycerol species. Microglial exposure to n-6 DPA stimulated expression of brain-derived neurotrophic factor ( BDNF ), which also tended to increase in microglia with reduced inflammatory marker expression when cultured in medium from ATRA-treated astrocytes. The results indicate that astrocyte-mediated n-6 DPA regulates the trophic functions of microglia in FXS.

title: Synergistic NiMn₂O₄@Biochar@CuBTC-MOF electrode for sensitive metformin detection: Insights from electrochemical and DFT analysis.
abstract: Metformin (MET) is a primary therapeutic for Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus; its environmental persistence and resistance to breakdown have raised concerns regarding long-term water contamination. Current studies demonstrate that the nanomaterial-based advanced functionalized sensors offer rapid, selective, and highly sensitive analytical solutions for environmental monitoring, food safety, and clinical diagnostics. This work aims to develop an effective electrochemical sensor for detecting MET using a nanocomposite material prepared by combining nickel manganite (NiMn 2 O 4 ) with biochar (BC) and Metal-Organic Framework (MOF), i.e., copper ions (Cu 2 ⁺) and 1,3,5-benzenetricarboxylic acid (BTC), CuBTC-MOF. In the prepared NiMn₂O₄@BC@CuBTC-MOF nanocomposite, NiMn₂O₄ provides enhanced electrical conductivity, BC offers structural stability, while CuBTC-MOF contributes high porosity. The resulting nanocomposite exhibited a BET surface area of ∼236.58 m 2 g -1 , a pore volume of ∼0.1752 cm 3 g -1 , and an average pore size of ∼2.96 nm, indicating a mesoporous structure favorable for electrochemical sensing. NiMn 2 O 4 @BC@CuBTC-MOF nanocomposite-modified sensing electrode showed a clear redox response, with a high oxidation current observed upon exposure to MET in an electrolyte. The experimental results demonstrated a reproducible sensitivity of ∼32.8462 μA/μM·cm 2 and an LOD of ∼10.8024 μM, with a good linear correlation (R 2 = ∼0.97838). title: A mid-throughput mitochondrial membrane potential assay in iPSC-derived RPE cells optimised for compound screening.
abstract: Age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is characterised by retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) dysfunction and degeneration, leading to secondary photoreceptor loss and central vision impairment. Mitochondrial dysfunction is implicated in AMD pathogenesis, making mitochondrial pathways attractive therapeutic targets. While induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived RPE cells are relevant to modelling this condition and for drug screening, intrinsic pigmentation complicates optical readouts and limits phenotypic screening. We optimised a mid-throughput, fluorescence-based assay to quantify mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm) in iPSC-derived RPE cells, using tetramethylrhodamine ethyl ester (TMRE), with conditions adapted to minimise pigment-associated signal interference and compatible with automated 96-well screening. Using a carbonyl cyanide 4-(trifluoromethoxy) phenylhydrazone(FCCP)-challenge paradigm, we screened 160 FDA-approved compounds and prioritised a small set of reproducible TMRE-preserving hits under FCCP-induced stress. Matched viability profiling indicated compound- and line-dependent cytotoxicity at some effective doses, supporting the need for orthogonal triage when interpreting TMRE rescue. Follow-up transcriptomic profiling by Multiplex Analysis of Cells sequencing (MAC-seq) revealed inter-line variability in transcriptional responses, including cases where functional ΔΨm preservation occurred with minimal or no detectable differential expression under the
summary_short: Age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is characterised by retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) dysfunction and degeneration, leading to secondary photoreceptor loss and central vision impairment. Mitochondrial dysfunction is implicated in AMD pathogenesis, making mitochondrial pathways attractive therapeutic targets.

title: Persistent metabolic remodeling after dietary salt reduction reveals sex differences in the adaptation to chronic high-salt intake.
abstract: Background Excessive salt intake is a risk factor for cardiovascular disease, yet its systemic metabolic consequences and its relationship to differential cardiovascular adaptations in males and females remain poorly understood. Here, we performed plasma metabolite profiling in male and female mice subjected to long-term high-salt diet (HSD) exposure during aging. Methods Mice were fed HSD (8.6% NaCl) or low-salt normal diet (ND; 0.6% NaCl) from 9 to 23 months of age, with a subset of mice undergoing diet reversal to ND after 7 months of HSD. Plasma metabolites were analyzed using gas chromatography/mass spectrometry and related to previously reported measurements of arterial blood pressure and cardiac function. Results Female mice developed salt-sensitive hypertension driven by vascular dysfunction, whereas male mice exhibited cardiac and vascular remodeling independent of blood pressure. Among 48 measured metabolites, HSD induced substantial alterations in levels of glucose, glycerol, glycerol phosphates, and fatty acids. Males showed a near-complete normalization of metabolite profiles following 7 months of salt reduction, whereas females retained a metabolomic signature different from ND despite normalization of blood pressure. In particular, metabolites related to energy metabolism, lipid handling, and osmotic balance were influenced by both diet and sex, with linoleate showing a significant sex-diet interaction. title: Chronic polystyrene nanoplastics exposure reprograms gene expression, alternative splicing, and disrupts host-microbiome-metabolic networks to promote atherosclerosis in LDLr⁻/⁻ mice.
abstract: Micro- and nanoplastics have been detected in human blood and carotid atheromas, yet their mechanistic contribution to atherogenesis is poorly defined, and chronic exposure studies of nanoplastics are limited. This multi-omics study investigates chronic (12-week) oral exposure to 80 nm polystyrene nanoplastics in LDLr⁻/⁻ mice, integrating aortic plaque quantification, hepatic transcriptomics with alternative splicing profiling, gut microbiome 16S sequencing, and liver untargeted metabolomics into a unified host-microbiome-metabolite network. Nanoplastics increased aortic lipid deposition, suppressed hepatic detoxification and anti-atherogenic lipid pathways at the transcriptional and post-transcriptional levels including alternative splicing events. Exposure induced gut dysbiosis, reduced SCFA-producing commensals and enriched pro-atherogenic pathobionts, shifts co-occurring directionally with hepatic transcriptional modules. Hepatic genes (down-regulated Fbp1, Ccn1 and Cyp2c29; upregulated Chka) and gut genera (depleted Bacteroides; enriched Faecalibaculum and Streptococcus) were confirmed by RT-qPCR and genus-specific qPCR. Untargeted metabolomics showed elevated aromatic and branched-chain amino acids such as tryptophan and methionine, and depletion of glutathione precursor γ-glutamylcysteine and the antioxidant taurine, implicating oxidative stress and amino-acid dysregulation. title: NeuroBase: A Web-Based Transcriptomic Resource and R Package for Cross-Disorder Analysis of Neurodegenerative and Neuropsychiatric Diseases.
abstract: Neurodegenerative and neuropsychiatric disorders, including Alzheimer's disease, autism spectrum disorder, bipolar disorder, Parkinson's disease, and schizophrenia, are highly prevalent and biologically complex conditions that remain difficult to diagnose and treat. This study aimed to develop NeuroBase, a web-based transcriptomic resource that supports exploratory comparison of shared and disorder-specific gene expression features across these disorders. Fourteen human brain bulk RNA sequencing datasets (262 total samples) were processed using a standardized pipeline, followed by differential gene expression analysis with DESeq2, edgeR and limma-voom for broad exploratory discovery, complemented by a multi-method sensitivity analysis to define a method-concordant core gene set, protein-protein interaction network analysis using STRING with downstream exploration in Cytoscape, and functional enrichment analysis. Principal component analysis and clustering-based visualizations were used to summarize similarities and differences in transcriptomic patterns among disorders. Differential expression analysis identified dataset-level significant genes within each disorder using DESeq2 for one dataset per disorder (FDR ≤ 0.05), including 38 genes in Alzheimer's disease, 6,704 in autism spectrum disorder, 3,559 in bipolar disorder, 687 in Parkinson's disease, and 2,750 in schizophrenia; a stricter multi-method intersection analysis yielded method-concordant Core Intersection sets in t

title: Variability in non-invasive tests: Challenges and implications for monitoring liver disease.
abstract: Background Diagnostic and prognostic non-invasive fibrosis tests (NITs) are increasingly repurposed to monitor liver disease. However, their reproducibility and the minimal detectable change (MDC, ie, the smallest change that exceeds expected measurement variability) are poorly characterized. Methods We retrospectively assessed variability of blood-based NITs and liver stiffness measurement (LSM) by vibration-controlled transient elastography on the same day (repeatability) and across use-cases when metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, fibrosis, or portal hypertension is suspected. Measurements were done within 90 days. Agreement and variability were quantified using intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC), Bland-Altman analyses, and MDC on the original (absolute) and relative (MDC%) scales. Results Across 6 cohorts, ICCs were generally good to excellent, but within-subject variability remained substantial. Same-day LSM had a pooled MDC% of 24% on the m/s scale, corresponding to an asymmetric kPa-equivalent window of -43% to +54%. For longitudinal lab-based NITs, pooled MDC% was 47% for FIB-4 and 56% for APRI, while absolute MDC was 13-17 percentage points for LiverPRO and 3 percentage points for CORE. Optimistic estimates remained substantial after excluding the 10% most extreme paired differences. title: Delays in screening, diagnosis and monitoring are associated with worse clinical and economic outcomes for patients with chronic kidney disease: a narrative review.
abstract: Background Chronic kidney disease (CKD) has substantial associated morbidity, mortality and healthcare costs that increase as CKD progresses. Despite newer, more effective treatments, the global burden of CKD continues to increase. Objective To understand patterns of screening, diagnosis, monitoring and treatment in CKD and how earlier treatment initiation could help mitigate CKD burden. Methods Targeted searches of bibliographic databases and grey literature sources identified studies published 2015-2025. Eligible evidence comprised observational studies on CKD screening and diagnosis rates, factors associated with delayed treatment initiation, clinical and economic burden of delayed diagnosis/treatment, and economic evaluations of population-based CKD screening. Thirty-five studies were synthesized narratively according to the CKD care pathway; no meta-analysis or formal quality assessment was conducted. Discussion Despite guideline recommendations, 19%-33% of patients in at-risk populations received neither kidney function nor albuminuria testing. Documented CKD diagnosis rates were often low, particularly in earlier stages. Documented CKD diagnosis was associated with increased monitoring and prescription fill rates, as well as slower decline of estimated glomerular filtration rate. title: Selective coil embolization of hepatic artery pseudoaneurysm causing hemobilia secondary to hemorrhagic hepatic hydatid cyst: A case report.
abstract: Hemobilia secondary to intrabiliary rupture of a hepatic hydatid cyst is rare, and concomitant arterial pseudoaneurysm formation further increases the risk of life-threatening hemorrhage. Case: An 80-year-old woman presented with 3 months of melena, progressing to large-volume melena and hematemesis. She was hypotensive and severely anemic (hemoglobin 6.0 g/dL). Upper endoscopy revealed a clot at the sphincter of Oddi, consistent with hemobilia. Multiphase CT showed a right-lobe hydatid cyst with active intracystic arterial extravasation and communication with the biliary ducts, with additional right-lobe hydatid cysts. Angiography identified a pseudoaneurysm arising from a segment V branch of the right hepatic artery. Given the patient's advanced age, hemodynamic instability, and high surgical risk, emergent selective endovascular embolization-rather than surgery-was chosen as first-line treatment, and superselective coil embolization achieved hemostasis. Post-procedure, hemoglobin improved to 10.6 g/dL by day 4; follow-up CT at day 4 demonstrated resolution of the pseudoaneurysm without rebleeding. Albendazole therapy was initiated after embolization. Echinococcus serology was not available, and reported follow-up was limited to 4 days; these are acknowledged as limitations. summary_short: Post-procedure, hemoglobin improved to 10.6 g/dL by day 4; follow-up CT at day 4 demonstrated resolution of the pseudoaneurysm without rebleeding.

title: Substrate-specific mitochondrial bioenergetics and metabolic flexibility in visceral adipose tissue across obesity-related glycemic states.
abstract: Obesity is characterized by the expansion of metabolically dysfunctional visceral adipose tissue (VAT) and chronic low-grade inflammation, which contribute to the development of insulin resistance. However, to what extent VAT bioenergetics and substrate preferences differ across distinct obesity-related glycaemic status profiles remains poorly understood. The present study aimed to assess substrate utilization and metabolic flexibility of VAT from individuals with obesity across different glycaemic statuses, namely euglycemia, prediabetes, and type 2 diabetes (T2D). VAT from individuals with obesity with euglycemia ( n = 11), prediabetes ( n = 12) and T2D ( n = 6) was harvested during bariatric surgery. VAT bioenergetics and mitochondrial substrate preferences under the influence of pyruvate, glutamine and fatty acids metabolism inhibitors, were assessed using the Seahorse Analyser. VAT expression of OB, GLS1, MPC1, CPT1a, HK2, PDHA1, RPII, β-actin genes was quantified by qRT-PCR. VAT basal mitochondrial respiration was similar across glycaemic groups. In VAT from euglycemic individuals, pyruvate inhibition decreased spare respiratory capacity. In contrast, in VAT from individuals with prediabetes and T2D, ATP-linked respiration increased when glutamine was the sole substrate available, which in individuals with prediabetes, was accompanied by an increase of non-mitochondrial oxygen consumption. title: Mapping the genetic landscape of microbial lipid transformation in the intestinal microbiome.
abstract: Dietary lipids are a key component in our diet, and fats and their derivatives have been associated with both beneficial as well as adverse effects on host health. However, the contribution of the gut microbiome to lipid metabolism remains understudied. Recognizing the importance of this interplay, we conducted extensive literature reviews to identify key bacterial genes involved in lipid metabolism, and created 88 Hidden Markov Models to allow rapid and accurate identification of these genes in genome and metagenome data. We applied these models to over 1000 metagenomes representative of the small intestine and colon, from both population-based and disease cohorts (LLDeep, MetaCardis and 1000IBD) to determine their lipolytic capacity. We observed that microbiome community types (enterotypes) carry different lipolytic potential. Serum levels of conjugated and sulfonated secondary bile acids were significantly associated with increased abundance of sterol-sulfonation genes ( cysC, cysD and BtSULT ). Small-intestinal communities were enriched in lipid genes compared to the colonic microbiota, underscoring the importance of microbial lipid metabolism in the small intestine compared to the colon. Overall, we demonstrate the value of our lipid metabolism models for functional microbiome profiling. Additionally, our study suggests that microbial activity in the upper gut might play a direct role in shaping host lipid metabolism, with potential implications for cardiometabolic healt

title: Energy drink consumption and associated lifestyle factors among German adolescents: findings from the EDKAR-study.
abstract: Purpose The consumption of energy drinks (EDs) has become increasingly popular among adolescents. The present study aimed to comprehensively characterize ED consumption behavior and associated lifestyle factors in pupils aged 15-18 years. Methods The cross-sectional EDKAR-study assessed data from 5100 German pupils using an online questionnaire. Following exclusion criteria, 4893 pupils were categorized into six ED consumer groups based on the frequency, duration, and quantity of their reported ED consumption: non-consumers, occasional, moderate, regular, chronic low, and chronic high consumers. Results Overall, 65.6% (n = 3208) reported ED consumption within the past 12 months, 12.6% on ≥ 4 days per week, and 3.9% daily. Median (IQR) daily ED intake was higher in groups with more frequent ED consumption, ranging from 20.5 ml/day (5.3-41.0) among occasional consumers to 818 ml/day (571-1250) among chronic high consumers. Reported adverse effects likewise increased from occasional to chronic high consumers, ranging from 23.2% to 50.2%, with palpitations, poor sleep, headaches, and chest pressure reported most frequently. Harmful lifestyle behaviors also increased from non-consumers to chronic high consumers, including alcohol intake (from 0.2 to 2.3 glasses per week), smoking rates (from 5.6% to 53.3%; cannabis: from 10.3% to 48.8%), short sleep duration ( 8 h/day: from 35.8% to 72.8%). title: Intracellular α<sub>1A</sub>-adrenergic receptor regulation of cAMP production by an inside-out mitogen-activated protein kinase signalling pathway in cardiac myocytes.
abstract: Sympathetic stimulation produces beneficial changes in cardiac function through β-adrenergic receptor (βAR) production of cAMP and subsequent alteration of electrical and mechanical activity. Long-term activation of cAMP production also contributes to cardiac remodelling and detrimental changes associated with heart failure. However, sympathetic responses are mediated by the endogenous neurotransmitter norepinephrine (NE), which is also a potent α 1 -adrenergic receptor (α 1 AR) agonist, and α 1 AR activation can produce significant effects on the heart as well. What is less clear is how α 1 - and β-adrenergic responses interact with one another. Previous studies have demonstrated that α 1 AR activation can inhibit β-adrenergic regulation of the electrical and mechanical activity of cardiac myocytes, although the signalling mechanisms involved were not previously known. In the present study, we used fluorescence resonance energy transfer (FRET)-based biosensors in adult rat ventricular myocytes to demonstrate that this cross-talk effect involves the inhibition of cAMP production by intracellular α 1A -adrenergic receptors (α 1A ARs) acting on βARs found on the plasma membrane. Furthermore, we established that this inside-out signalling mechanism involves a mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway that uncouples βARs from downstream signalling in a G protein-coupled receptor kinase (GRK)/arrestin-dependent manner.
