title: GLP-1 based therapy of obesity and type 2 diabetes.
abstract: GLP-1 is 30-amino acid peptide that is secreted from the intestine in response to food intake. The release mechanism involves luminal exposure to as well as absorption and metabolism of the major nutrients. It functions mainly as a part of the ileal brake mechanism whereby nutrient entry in distal segments of the small intestine inhibit gastrointestinal secretion and motility as well as appetite and food intake, signalling nutritional abundance. It also functions as a second line incretin hormone. It acts on the brain via sensory vagal afferents, but also interacts with exposed neurons expressing the GLP-1 receptor in the circumventricular organs, in turn activating brain nuclei involved in appetite regulation and reward. High doses of GLP-1 cause nausea and vomiting, but slow dosing titration mitigates this. GLP-1 Receptor Agonists owe their actions to these physiological mechanisms and therefore represent powerful antidiabetic agents (A1c levels below 5.7%) and cause major weight loss (up to 20%), but also appear to reduce the systemic low-grade inflammation of obesity and type 2 diabetes and to exert beneficial action on the blood vessels, providing the GLP-1RAs with preventive effects on cardiovascular, hepatic, renal and central nervous system complications. Orally active GLP-1rAs have also been developed. It is emphasized that GLP-1RA therapy should be accompanied by lifestyle changes for efficacy and to prevent side effects of the weight loss. title: Associations of fibroblast growth factor 21 with renal parameter changes during pemafibrate treatment in patients with type 2 diabetes.
abstract: Background Experimental studies suggest that fibroblast growth factor 21 (FGF21) is involved in pathways related to peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor alpha (PPARα) activation, whereas elevated circulating FGF21 has also been associated with metabolic stress and kidney dysfunction. We examined the associations of FGF21 with renal parameter changes following the initiation of pemafibrate, a selective PPARα modulator, in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM). Methods In this retrospective study using prospectively collected blood samples, 81 patients with T2DM who initiated pemafibrate and continued treatment for ≥ 2 years were analyzed. Clinical data and serum high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hsCRP) and FGF21 levels were assessed at baseline and two years. The main outcomes were changes in estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) and log-transformed urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR). Multivariable linear regression analyses were performed. Results During the two-year observation period, triglyceride, hsCRP, and UACR levels decreased, whereas FGF21 increased; eGFR remained stable. The change in eGFR was more favorable in patients with baseline eGFR of 30 to 2 than in those with eGFR ≥ 60 mL/min/1.73 m 2 . Higher baseline FGF21 and greater increases in FGF21 remained associated with less favorable changes in eGFR and UACR in multivariable analyses. title: <i>Rhodotorula mucilaginosa</i> DM2025 ameliorates obesity through cholesterol binding and the gut mycobiome-BAT PPARγ/UCP1 axis.
abstract: Obesity is a major global health challenge, necessitating safe and effective therapies. Although probiotics are promising for obesity management, research has focused on bacteria, leaving non- Saccharomyces yeasts underexplored. Here, we investigated the anti‑obesity mechanisms of Rhodotorula mucilaginosa DM2025, isolated from the healthy murine gut. To test whether benefits depend on viable cells, high‑fat diet‑fed mice received either live yeast or its cell‑free supernatant, followed by integrated physiological, genomic, and metabolomic analyzes. Live yeast, but not supernatant, significantly reduced body weight gain, improved serum lipids, and was associated with activation of brown adipose tissue thermogenesis (upregulated PPARγ, PGC1α, UCP1). Though the supernatant lowered total cholesterol, it failed to affect weight or thermogenic genes, indicating cholesterol‑lowering and weight reduction are distinct processes. Live cells were enriched in propionate, indole, and carotenoid‑related metabolites, with genomic support for their biosynthesis. Live yeast reshaped the gut mycobiome, promoting Basidiomycota / Rhodotorula dominance; this fungal restructuring was absent in HFD controls. These findings suggest that R. mucilaginosa DM2025 anti‑obesity efficacy relies on the continuous metabolic activity of live cells, producing thermogenesis‑associated metabolites that may contribute to BAT activation. title: Oncogenic mechanisms and therapeutic potential of SALL4 in hematological malignancies (Review).
abstract: As a member of the spalt like transcription factor (SALL) family, SALL4 regulates multiple oncogenic processes including cell proliferation, metastasis, epithelial-mesenchymal transition, cancer stem cell maintenance and drug resistance. Physiologically, it is essential for the self-renewal of embryonic and hematopoietic stem cells. Aberrant upregulation of SALL4 is frequently observed in both solid tumors and hematological malignancies; it has been proven to play a critical role in hematological malignancies, especially acute myeloid leukemia, acute lymphoblastic leukemia, myelodysplastic syndrome, chronic myeloid leukemia and mixed-lineage leukemia, where it promotes malignant cell proliferation, disease progression, and chemoresistance via downstream genes and key signaling pathways. Targeting key oncogenic molecules represents a promising therapeutic strategy for hematological malignancies. Elucidating the regulatory mechanisms of SALL4 may identify a novel therapeutic target. The present review summarizes the regulatory functions of SALL4 on key oncogenic targets and its upregulation profile in hematological malignancies. Although some mechanisms are mainly illustrated in solid tumors, they provide important insights for hematological cancer. Overall, SALL4 exhibits great potential as a novel therapeutic target and prognostic biomarker for hematological malignancies.

title: Correlation between proteinuria and cardiac biomarker levels in kidney transplant recipients.
abstract: Kidney transplantation is the preferred treatment for end-stage kidney disease, with improved short-term outcomes; however, long-term graft and patient survival remain suboptimal. Proteinuria is a strong predictor of adverse graft and cardiovascular outcomes. We investigated the relationship between proteinuria and selected cardiac and inflammatory biomarkers, including the interleukin-33 (IL-33)/soluble ST2 (sST2) axis, malondialdehyde, neprilysin, growth differentiation factor-15 (GDF-15), and angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2), in kidney transplant recipients, with a focus on patients with heart failure. Methods: Sixty-five transplant recipients were included: 15 kidney transplant recipients with heart failure and 49 controls consisting of kidney or heart transplant recipients without heart failure. Patients were followed between November 2023 and June 2024 at the Division of Nephrology at the University of Debrecen. Proteinuria was assessed using the urinary protein-to-creatinine ratio. Laboratory analyses included routine biochemical parameters, inflammatory markers, NT-proBNP, soluble IL-33 receptor (sST2), neprilysin, GDF-15, and ACE2 activity. Discrete data were described as percentages and analyzed with Fisher's exact test. Group comparisons were performed using the Kruskal-Wallis test, and correlations were assessed using non-parametric methods. title: Inhibitory effects of the bone marrow microenvironment on erythroid progenitors in pure red cell aplasia.
abstract: Background Primary pure red cell aplasia (PRCA) is a rare hematologic disorder characterized by severe anemia and selective erythroid hypoplasia in the bone marrow. While immune-mediated mechanisms are central to its pathogenesis, the role of soluble inflammatory factors in the bone marrow microenvironment remains poorly understood. Methods Bone marrow plasma and lineage-negative (Lin - ) hematopoietic progenitor cells were obtained from untreated PRCA patients and healthy controls. K562 erythroleukemia cells were co-cultured with plasma and induced to undergo erythroid differentiation using hemin. Hemoglobin production was assessed by benzidine staining, and GATA1/GATA2 protein expression was analyzed by Western blotting. Erythroid colony-forming assays were performed to quantify small and large burst-forming unit-erythroid (BFU-E) and colony-forming unit-erythroid (CFU-E) colonies. Cytokine levels in bone marrow supernatant were measured. The effects of dexamethasone, cyclosporine A, and rapamycin on colony formation were also evaluated. Results PRCA bone marrow plasma significantly inhibited hemoglobinization in K562 cells and suppressed GATA2 expression without affecting GATA1. Lin - cells from PRCA patients formed markedly fewer large BFU-E colonies than those from controls. title: Distinct associations of <i>STK11</i> rs2301759 and <i>SLC29A4</i> rs2685753 with metformin response among Saudi patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus.
abstract: Aims This study investigates the genotype and allele frequencies of solute carrier family 29 member 4 ( SLC29A4) rs2685753 and serine/threonine kinase 11 ( STK11) rs2301759 in the Saudi population and their association with metformin response in Saudi patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), while comparing the findings with other ethnic populations. Patients & methods A prospective cohort study included 69 newly diagnosed Saudi adults with T2DM receiving metformin monotherapy for at least six months and 59 healthy controls. Genotyping was performed using TaqMan single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) assays. Associations between genetic variants and glycemic response were analyzed using chi-square tests and logistic regression. Results Among patients, 55% achieved adequate glycemic control, whereas 45% were non-responders. SLC29A4 rs2685753 showed no significant association with the metformin response. In contrast, STK11 rs2301759 demonstrated significant genotypic and allelic associations, with the C/T genotype linked to improved glycemic response. Higher baseline glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) and family history of diabetes were associated with poorer response. Conclusion STK11 rs2301759 may influence metformin efficacy in Saudi patients with T2DM and could support personalized diabetes management.
summary_short: In contrast, STK11 rs2301759 demonstrated significant genotypic and allelic associations, with the C/T genotype linked to improved glycemic response. Higher baseline glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) and family history of diabetes were associated with poorer response.

title: Hyperinsulinemia contributes to regulatory T-cell dysfunction and disease activity in multiple sclerosis.
abstract: We examined relationships among obesity, hyperinsulinemia, regulatory T-cell (Treg) function, and activity in multiple sclerosis (MS), and investigated insulin signaling as a candidate mechanism. We prospectively followed 131 patients with relapsing-remitting MS, stratified by body mass index, for at least 36 months. Clinical and MRI outcomes were assessed longitudinally, whereas metabolic parameters and Treg phenotype and function were evaluated at baseline. Mechanistic studies examined insulin receptor signaling in purified Tregs using insulin stimulation, pharmacological inhibition, insulin receptor silencing, and functional assays. In a separate, non-overlapping cohort, 28 obese hyperinsulinemic patients with relapsing-remitting MS underwent a 24-week metformin intervention with longitudinal metabolic and immunological assessments. Obese patients had higher fasting insulin, more relapses, disability progression, and MRI activity. Hyperinsulinemia correlated with reduced FoxP3 and IL-10, impaired Treg suppression, and increased IFN-γ and IL-17 in Treg-enriched cultures. Insulin stimulation altered AKT-mTOR signaling and Treg function; AKT inhibition or insulin receptor silencing reversed these effects. Obese-patient Tregs suppressed myelin-reactive responses less effectively. During metformin treatment, reductions in fasting insulin and AKT-mTOR signaling were accompanied by improvements in Treg phenotype and suppressive function and attenuation of myelin-specific inflamma
summary_short: Hyperinsulinemia correlated with reduced FoxP3 and IL-10, impaired Treg suppression, and increased IFN-γ and IL-17 in Treg-enriched cultures.

title: Guanidinium-driven fluorescence detection of microcystins using carbon dot embedded silica nanoparticles.
abstract: Detection of microcystins in environmental waters is constrained by complex analytical methods and the cost of whole-toxin-based imprinting techniques. Herein, we report a carbon-dot-embedded silica molecularly imprinted polymer (CDSiMIP) nanosensor prepared using L-arginine as a surrogate fragment template. The Arg-CDSiMIP nanosensor showed preferential fluorescence responses toward guanidyl-bearing microcystins, achieving detection limits of 33 ng L -1 for microcystin-LR (0-450 ng L -1 ) and 13 ng L -1 for microcystin-RR (0-400 ng L -1 ) with an interaction/response time of 15 min. Substantial microcystin-LR-induced quenching was maintained over a pH range of 6.0-10.0, whereas environmental interferents, free amino acids, and a photosynthetic pigment extract produced comparatively lower responses. In spiked lake water, fluorescence-based recoveries were 105%-117% (relative standard deviation ≤1.5%), with concentration estimates generally comparable to those obtained by independent mass spectrometric measurements. These findings establish the fragment-imprinted CDSiMIP nanosensor as a sensitive, rapid optical screening platform for detecting microcystins in environmental water.
summary_short: Herein, we report a carbon-dot-embedded silica molecularly imprinted polymer (CDSiMIP) nanosensor prepared using L-arginine as a surrogate fragment template.

title: Knowledge, Attitudes, and Practices Regarding the Long-Term Health Risks of Energy Drink Consumption Among Adults in Iraq: A Cross-Sectional Study.
abstract: Background and aims Energy drink consumption is common among young adults, yet evidence on knowledge, attitudes and practices in Iraq remains limited. This study assessed these domains among adults in Iraq and examined associations of knowledge and risk concern with past-year use and consumption frequency. Methods A cross-sectional online survey was conducted in Iraq from May to November 2025 using a structured Arabic questionnaire distributed through social media. The sample included 1125 adults. Scale reliability and construct validity were assessed using ordinal alpha coefficients and confirmatory factor analysis. Structural equation models examined associations of knowledge and risk concern with past-year energy drink use and consumption frequency, adjusting for demographic covariates. Results Past-year consumption was reported by 399/1125 participants (35.5%). Of the 1125 participants, 1002 (89.1%) identified arrhythmias, 977 (86.8%) sleep problems and 794 (70.6%) raised blood pressure as potential risks; 468 (41.6%) reported knowing the ingredients. Support for warning labels, awareness campaigns and age restrictions was 1029/1125 (91.5%), 1023/1125 (90.9%) and 974/1125 (86.6%), respectively. Higher knowledge was associated with greater risk concern, which was associated with a lower likelihood of past-year use and lower consumption frequency among consumers. title: Targeting mitochondrial quality control to disarm phytopathogenic fungi.
abstract: Fungal diseases cause substantial crop losses worldwide, while increasing fungicide resistance highlights the need for new disease-control strategies. Mitochondrial quality control (MQC), comprising mitochondrial dynamics, biogenesis, proteostasis, and mitophagy, maintains mitochondrial integrity and functional capacity during infection. Evidence from phytopathogenic fungi links disruption of individual MQC mechanisms to defects in growth, stress adaptation, and pathogenicity. Here, we synthesize evidence across hemibiotrophic, vascular, and necrotrophic pathogens and across distinct stages of the infection cycle. Because mechanistic evidence is strongest in Magnaporthe oryzae , we use it as a principal reference system while highlighting conserved and lifestyle-specific requirements emerging from other fungi. This review proposes three complementary strategies for exploiting MQC vulnerabilities: targeting pathogen-specific regulatory features within conserved mitochondrial systems, exploiting interdependencies among MQC processes and mitochondrial stress responses, and targeting stage-specific mitochondrial requirements as potential intervention points. We also highlight some limitations that need resolution while considering MQC mechanisms as antifungal targets.

title: Perioperative Management of a Breastfed Child Whose Mother Was Receiving Injectable Semaglutide: A Case Report Outlining Use of Gastric Point-of-Care Ultrasound.
abstract: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs), including semaglutide, are increasingly used for the treatment of type 2 diabetes mellitus and for weight management. Although generally effective, specific end-organ effects, including delayed gastric emptying, may impact the perioperative care of patients receiving these agents. Given these concerns, guidelines have been suggested for the perioperative care of patients receiving GLP-1 RAs. However, these recommendations do not specifically address the increasingly encountered scenario in which a breastfeeding mother is taking a GLP-1 RA and the breastfed infant or young child is presenting for anesthetic care. We present a 15-month-old breastfed child who presented for surgery and whose mother was receiving once-weekly injectable semaglutide. Given limited evidence-based medicine to guide perioperative care in this clinical scenario, preoperative gastric point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) was used to evaluate gastric volume before induction of anesthesia. Perioperative care of breastfed children of mothers receiving GLP-1 RAs is discussed, the role of gastric POCUS is presented, and options for perioperative care are reviewed.

title: Polydopamine-coated liposomes for oral delivery of tirzepatide: Overcoming gastrointestinal barriers to improve therapeutic efficacy.
abstract: Tirzepatide (TZP), the first dual GIP/GLP-1 receptor agonist, offers substantial therapeutic benefits for type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) but remains confined to subcutaneous injection. While oral delivery of peptide therapeutics improves patient compliance, it is severely hampered by enzymatic degradation and mucosal barriers in the gastrointestinal tract. Liposomes, as biocompatible nanocarriers, can protect encapsulated drugs, enhance intestinal stability, and enable controlled release. Herein, TZP-loaded liposomes (TZP-Lip) were prepared via reverse-phase evaporation and further coated with polydopamine (PDA) to obtain TZP-Lip@PDA for enhanced oral delivery. TZP-Lip@PDA exhibited an encapsulation efficiency of 95.02 ± 1.14%, a particle size of 145.9 ± 1.49 nm, and preservation of the secondary structure of TZP. The PDA coating functioned as a physical diffusion barrier that conferred sustained-release behavior in simulated gastrointestinal fluids, while enhancing mucus penetration and promoting cellular uptake in Caco-2 cells. Pharmacokinetic studies showed that oral TZP-Lip@PDA achieved measurable plasma exposure, whereas oral free TZP remained below the lower limit of quantification (LLOQ, 5 ng/mL). Despite a tenfold higher dose (8.8 vs 0.88 mg/kg), oral TZP-Lip@PDA achieved a Cmax approximately 50% of that observed after subcutaneous administration of free TZP, within the 12-h sampling window, indicating substantial progress but also the remaining quantitative gap betw
summary_short: Liposomes, as biocompatible nanocarriers, can protect encapsulated drugs, enhance intestinal stability, and enable controlled release.

title: Usefulness of Phase Angle as an Overall Marker of Muscle Health in Older Patients With Type 2 Diabetes.
abstract: Background Sarcopenia is characterized by deterioration of muscle health, loss of muscle mass and strength, and decline of physical performance. Thus, measurement of these markers is needed for the assessment of muscle health. Muscle mass is easily measured by a bioelectrical impedance analysis (BIA) or dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA), but measurement of muscle strength and physical performance requires trained personnel and specialized settings. Cross-sectional analyses have demonstrated that the phase angle (PhA), which is directly obtained from a BIA, is associated with muscle mass, muscle strength, and the physical function in healthy individuals and patients with type 2 diabetes. However, longitudinal associations between the PhA and these muscle markers have not been fully investigated, and the clinical usefulness of the PhA in patients with type 2 diabetes remains unclear. Therefore, we performed a retrospective longitudinal analysis of changes in PhA, muscle mass and strength, and physical performance over 3 years. Methods We analyzed the associations between the PhA and muscle-related parameters in 101 patients with type 2 diabetes without sarcopenia (61 men, 40 women; age at baseline: 60-85 years). We assessed the PhA, appendicular skeletal muscle index (SMI), handgrip strength, leg extension strength, and Short Physical Performance Battery (SPPB) scores at baseline and after 3 years. title: Effects of vacuum-packaged stewing on the quality stability and flavor characteristics of chicken soup during storage.
abstract: This study investigated the effects of vacuum-packaged stewing (VPS) on the quality stability and flavor characteristics of chicken soup with Polygonatum sibiricum during refrigerated storage (4 °C). Both VPS and traditional stewing (TS) samples were vacuum-packaged during storage. Compared with TS, VPS showed lower thiobarbituric acid reactive substances (TBARS) and total volatile basic nitrogen (TVB-N) values during storage. At 20 d, VPS exhibited higher overall sensory acceptability than TS (7.80 ± 0.05 vs. 7.15 ± 0.10). VPS also exhibited higher concentrations of umami amino acids, total free amino acids (2556.60 ± 38.46 vs. 2207.43 ± 38.97 mg/L), and total dipeptides (4608.58 ± 69.26 vs. 3750.09 ± 55.22 mg/L) than TS at 20 d, with these differences remaining significant after soup-yield normalization. Gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS) and gas chromatography-ion mobility spectrometry (GC-IMS) identified 20 and 37 volatile compounds, with aldehydes predominating in both analyses. During storage, GC-MS-derived aldehyde concentrations and GC-IMS-derived total aldehyde peak volumes decreased in TS, whereas aldehyde concentrations remained unchanged and total aldehyde peak volumes increased in VPS. Overall, VPS shows potential for improving quality stability and maintaining desirable sensory characteristics of prepared chicken soup during refrigerated storage.

title: Age-Related Alterations in Human Gut Microbiota and Intestinal Aging: Microbial Signatures, Disease Associations and Intervention Strategies.
abstract: Aging is accompanied by progressive alterations in gut homeostasis, characterized by gut microbiota dysbiosis, impaired intestinal barrier function, immune dysregulation, and chronic low-grade inflammation. Increasing evidence indicates that age-related gut microbial remodeling is closely associated with the development of multiple age-associated disorders, including frailty, sarcopenia, cardiovascular diseases, and neurodegenerative diseases. However, existing reviews have primarily focused on individual aspects of gut microbiota-mediated aging, whereas a systematic framework integrating gut microbial dysbiosis, intestinal aging, and the development of multiple age-related diseases through shared pathogenic mechanisms remains lacking. This review provides a comprehensive synthesis of age-related alterations in human gut microbiota, with particular emphasis on bacterial taxa consistently associated with healthy aging and age-related diseases. We further integrate current evidence to examine the associations between age-related microbial alterations and intestinal aging, with particular attention to microbial function, barrier integrity, and host immune responses. Finally, we review microbiota-targeted interventions, including fecal microbiota transplantation, probiotics, prebiotics, and dietary modulation, and discuss their potential and limitations in promoting healthy aging. title: Whole-Genome Resequencing Reveals Genetic Diversity and Selection Signatures in Honghe Cattle.
abstract: Honghe cattle were formally recognized as the eighth indigenous cattle breed in Yunnan Province, a region in southwestern China characterized by complex geography and variable climates that have shaped distinctive local cattle germplasm. In this study, we generated whole-genome resequencing data from 62 Honghe cattle and compared them with additional reference samples from other breeds. The results revealed that Honghe cattle are predominantly of indicine origin (54.7% East Asian indicine, 26.5% South Asian indicine and 18.8% taurine), with relatively high genetic diversity. Runs of homozygosity analysis revealed low inbreeding (F ROH = 0.032) and identified 52 ROH islands, the strongest of which (chr7) harbored a protein homeostasis gene cluster ( HSPA9 , SIL1 , DNAJC18 ). For selection signatures, we applied multiple methods, including composite likelihood ratio test (CLR), integrated haplotype score ( iHS ), fixation index ( F ST ) and cross-population extended haplotype homozygosity (XP-EHH) to identify selective sweeps in the Honghe cattle genome. We detected several candidate genes associated with important traits, such as HMGA2 (body size) and MCM6 (milk production). Functional enrichment analyses revealed pathways related to immune response, protein absorption, energy metabolism, and lipid metabolism. title: Partial Replacement of Fish Meal with Tuna By-Product Meal, Black Soldier Fly Larvae Meal, Fermented Soybean Meal, and Their Two Combinations in Olive Flounder (<i>Paralichthys olivaceus</i>) Diets: Effects on Growth, Feed Utilization, Biochemical Composition, and Economic Analysis.
abstract: Fish meal (FM) remains a primary protein source in aquafeeds; however, its high cost and limited availability necessitate the exploration of alternative protein sources. This study, thus, investigates the effects of replacing 10% FM protein, equivalent to 22.2% of FM, with tuna by-product meal (TBM), black soldier fly ( Hermetia illucens ) larvae meal (BSF), fermented soybean meal (FSB), and their two combinations in diets on the growth, feed utilization, and biochemical composition of olive flounder ( P. olivaceus ), as well as on economic efficiency. A total of 450 juveniles averaging 10.3 g were randomly distributed into 18 300 L flow-through tanks (25 juveniles per tank). In the control (Con) diet (45% FM-basal), 10% FM protein was replaced with TBM, BSF, FSB, or a combination of TBM and BSF or TBM and FSB at a 1:1 ratio, referred to as the TBM, BSF, FSB, CTB, and CTF diets, respectively. Each experimental diet was randomly allocated to three replicate groups of fish. The fish were hand-fed to apparent satiation twice daily for 12 weeks. The weight gain, specific growth rate, feed consumption, and feed efficiency of fish fed the TBM diet were comparable to those fed the Con diet, but significantly higher than those fed the BSF, FSB, CTB, and CTF diets. The protein efficiency ratio of fish fed the TBM diet was significantly higher than that of fish fed the FSB diet. title: Multi-omics, spatial omics and artificial intelligence in chronic diseases: current applications and future directions.
abstract: Chronic diseases exhibit multiscale heterogeneity and spatial organization, yet analytical frameworks often fail to connect molecular perturbations, tissue architecture, and clinical outcomes within a unified evidence framework. Bulk and single-modality approaches can identify regulatory or cellular alterations but provide limited insight into why pathogenic programs emerge in anatomical regions, how they shape disease niches, and how they drive divergent clinical trajectories. Multi-omics partially addresses this gap by resolving interconnected layers of regulation, transcription, protein activity, and metabolism, whereas spatial omics maps these processes within preserved tissue architecture, enabling the delineation of lesion topology, interface states, and multicellular microenvironments. Artificial intelligence (AI) may further extend this framework by integrating molecular, spatial, imaging, and clinical data into disease representations that support disease stratification, the discovery of mechanistic patterns, and clinically testable predictions, provided that models are externally validated, biologically interpretable, and robust to dataset bias and domain shift. In this review, we examine how multi-omics, spatial omics, and AI can bridge the disconnect between molecular profiling, spatial pathology, and clinical translation in chronic disease research. title: Efficient Plasma and Placenta Metabolic Fingerprints for Preeclampsia Diagnosis: A Multicenter Study.
abstract: Preeclampsia (PE) is a leading cause of maternal and perinatal mortality. There remains a clinical need for accurate and accessible diagnostic approaches to facilitate timely identification of PE. Herein, the nanoparticle-enhanced laser desorption/ionization mass spectrometry is applied to obtain plasma ( n = 236) and placenta ( n = 70) metabolic fingerprints from a multicenter dataset (109 PE patients and 127 non-PE participants, 4 centers). Diagnostic models are constructed with an efficient diagnostic area under the curve (AUC) of 0.941 with external validation. Subsequently, 19 PE-associated metabolites are annotated, demonstrating good diagnostic performance with an AUC of 0.871. Moreover, diagnostic scores of severe PE patients are significantly higher than those of PE patients, exhibiting our model's capacity to differentiate disease severity. Related metabolic pathways are revealed to inform potential therapeutic strategies for PE and biological validation on trophoblast cells demonstrates that key biomarkers, including L-alanine, taurine, hypoxanthine, and orotic acid, can significantly enhance migration capabilities ( p < 0.01). This work highlights the potential of metabolic analysis for PE detection, paving the way for improved clinical decision-making in obstetrics.

abstract: Sexual health counseling is a critical yet under-addressed component of cardiac rehabilitation following post-percutaneous coronary intervention. Although nurses' positive attitudes-particularly regarding role responsibility and comfort with sexual health discussions-and their readiness to provide clinical sexual counseling can facilitate patient care, translating professional knowledge into practice is often hindered by specific constraints and complex sociocultural norms. A cross-sectional, explanatory correlational study. Four tertiary-level percutaneous coronary intervention centers within the Bangkok metropolitan administration network, Bangkok, Thailand. title: Deubiquitinases in cancer: biology, mechanism, and therapeutic targeting.
abstract: The ubiquitin-proteasome system (UPS) plays a central role in cellular protein homeostasis by regulating the degradation, trafficking, and activity of target proteins. Deubiquitinases (DUBs) are a crucial component of this regulatory network, catalyzing the removal of ubiquitin moieties from modified substrates to modulate signaling pathways that govern cell cycle control, apoptosis, DNA repair, immune responses, and stress adaptation. Aberrant DUB expression or activity is increasingly recognized as a driver of oncogenesis, tumor progression, drug resistance, and metastasis. As a result, DUBs have emerged as novel therapeutic targets in cancer, complementing existing proteasome inhibitors. This review provides an overview of DUB classification, their mechanistic roles in cancer biology, current progress in small-molecule DUB inhibitors and DUB-directed PROTACs, and discusses translational challenges and future opportunities for therapeutic development.

title: Craniofacial Load Modifies the Interaction of Obesity and Apnea Hypopnea Index Severity in Adult Males.
abstract: Objectives Multiple physiological, skeletal structural, and BMI variables determine obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) severity. To better understand how craniofacial, hyoid, and obesity measures interact, data from a population-based study was re-evaluated. Methods Lateral facial cephalometric and polysomnographic data (2% desaturation criteria for hypopnea) were reanalyzed from a population-based study and enhanced clinic population (Wisconsin Cohort Study). Cephalometric x-rays were performed awake, upright, at end expiration. Data on craniofacial structure (45 craniofacial, 10 hyoid related), age, and obesity were re-evaluated using linear and non-linear logarithmic methods. Residual variance was assessed with hierarchical cluster analysis and classified with linear discriminant analysis. Results 203 male patients (141 population based and 62 clinic) were included (female numbers were inadequate and were excluded from analysis). Linear analysis of all variables explained 41.3% of AHI variance with two primary contributors of BMI (28.5%) and lower facial width (12.8%). AHI at higher levels remained unexplained. Subsequent non-linear analysis identified 3 statistical groups differing in cephalometric, age, and BMI variables contributing to AHI. Clinically, the 3 groups differed in craniofacial and hyoid (1.4%, 42%, and 67%) and BMI contributions (87.6%, 40.4%, and 19.3%) and described low, intermediate, and high levels of craniofacial load. title: Effectiveness of incretin receptor agonists compared to metreleptin in partial lipodystrophy: a retrospective study.
abstract: Context Lipodystrophy syndromes are rare disorders of abnormal fat distribution and metabolic disease. The only approved therapy for generalized lipodystrophy is recombinant leptin (metreleptin), which is not approved for partial lipodystrophy. Recent data suggest efficacy of glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists and glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist/glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP) dual agonists (collectively referred to as incretins) to treat complications of lipodystrophy. Objective To compare metabolic outcomes of incretin therapies vs metreleptin in partial lipodystrophy. Design Retrospective review of patients who received metreleptin as part of a clinical trial and incretins during routine care under a natural history study. Setting NIH Clinical Center. Patients Twelve female patients with partial lipodystrophy, aged 16-85 years. All but 1 patient had diabetes. Intervention Eleven patients with partial lipodystrophy were treated with metreleptin (mean duration 104 ± 38 months) before switching to incretin therapy (duration 32 ± 13 months). A twelfth patient took metreleptin and an incretin concurrently. Main outcome measures Outcome measures included hemoglobin A1c, insulin dose, Matsuda index, insulinogenic index, disposition index, fasting glucose and insulin, homeostatic model of beta cell function (HOMA-B), homeostatic model assessment of insulin resistance (HOMA-IR), weight, lipids, liver elastography, and liver steatosis. title: Guideline-directed medical therapy use, persistence, and cardiovascular outcomes following ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction: a pooled analysis of three randomised trials with external registry validation.
abstract: Background Implementation and long-term persistence of guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) following ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) remain suboptimal. We assessed the implementation and persistence of four-class GDMT after STEMI and its association with outcomes. Methods We performed a patient-level pooled analysis of three randomised trials of patients undergoing percutaneous coronary intervention for STEMI. GDMT was defined by the number of drug classes prescribed (0-4). External validation was conducted using a real-world PCI registry. Findings The study included 2270 patients from the randomised trials and 5643 from a real-world PCI registry. More than two-thirds of patients received all four GDMT classes at discharge (ranging from 66.9% [398/595] to 83.5% [339/406]), but this proportion declined over 5 years (ranging from 40.5% [408/1008] to 53.1% [276/520]). title: Quercetin: sources, absorption, metabolism, and gut microbiota interactions.
abstract: Quercetin is a widely occurring dietary flavonol with documented health effects. It can be obtained from a range of plant sources, synthesized chemically, and generated through microbial biosynthesis in engineered bacterial hosts. Upon ingestion, quercetin is absorbed mainly via passive transcellular diffusion across the intestinal epithelium, while unabsorbed fractions reach the colon. The absorbed quercetin undergoes Phase II conjugation catalyzed by UGTs (UDP-glucuronosyltransferases), SULTs (sulfotransferases), and COMT (catechol- O -methyltransferase) in the liver and intestine, generating circulating conjugates. In the colon, unabsorbed quercetin bidirectionally interacts with the microbiota. It reduces LPS-producing Gram-negative bacteria, promotes short-chain fatty acid production, and modulates bile acid and tryptophan metabolism. Conversely, gut microbiota cleave the quercetin C-ring and perform secondary modifications (dehydroxylation, decarboxylation, and methylation) to generate bioactive phenolic catabolites, which exhibit multiple activities. Understanding the sources, absorption, metabolism, and gut microbiota interactions of quercetin is essential for optimizing its therapeutic and nutritional applications.

title: Functional divergence within mulberry-associated <i>Pantoea ananatis</i>: Insights from comparative genomics and host-contact metabolomics.
abstract: Pantoea ananatis is a widely distributed plant-associated bacterium that can exhibit contrasting ecological functions, ranging from plant-beneficial activities to pathogenicity. However, the genomic and metabolic features associated with such functional divergence among closely related strains remain poorly understood. Here, we characterized 18 mulberry-associated P. ananatis isolates using phenotypic assays and selected Pa-6 and YSFJ as representatives of two predominant functional types for comparative genomic and host-contact metabolomic analyses. Pa-6 exhibited a beneficial-associated phenotype characterized by several plant growth-promoting and antagonistic traits, comparatively limited tissue damage, and lower disease severity during the later stages of co-inoculation with Ralstonia pseudosolanacearum XZqk. In contrast, YSFJ caused progressive wilt accompanied by bacterial aggregation, xylem occlusion, vascular disorganization, and tissue damage. Despite these contrasting phenotypes, Pa-6 and YSFJ shared approximately 98.9% average nucleotide identity. Comparative genomic analyses revealed differences in accessory-gene content, plasmid composition, and strain-specific homologous clusters. Annotation comparisons highlighted a GH19-associated locus in Pa-6 and wbpZ- and feoB-associated loci in YSFJ as putative gene-content differences. title: LncRNA-Mediated Regulation of Hepatic Metabolic Homeostasis: Cholesterol, Triglyceride, Glucose and Pathological Implications.
abstract: The liver coordinately maintains cholesterol, triglyceride, and glucose homeostasis by integrating the synthesis, storage, utilization, and inter-conversion of these metabolic programs, and their dysregulation contributes to metabolic-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), and gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM). Long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs), which are not translated into proteins, regulate gene expression through interactions with DNA, RNA, and proteins at transcriptional, post-transcriptional, and epigenetic levels, and have emerged as central determinants of hepatic metabolic balance. This review systematically summarizes how lncRNAs govern cholesterol biosynthesis and efflux, triglyceride synthesis and lipolysis, glycogen turnover, gluconeogenesis, and glycolysis in hepatocytes. Unlike pathway-by-pathway descriptions, we highlight that these programs are coupled through shared signaling networks, including PI3K/AKT/mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1), 5'-AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK), SREBP, PPAR, and FoxO1, and that pleiotropic lncRNAs coordinate lipid and glucose outputs rather than controlling a single isolated process. We further examine how lncRNA dysregulation drives MASLD, HCC, T2DM, and GDM, and evaluate their potential as diagnostic biomarkers and therapeutic targets. title: Engineering <i>in vitro</i> models of liver fibrosis.
abstract: Liver fibrosis is a progressive and potentially life-threatening condition arising from chronic hepatic injury, characterized by the aberrant accumulation of extracellular matrix (ECM) driven by activated hepatic stellate cells (HSCs). The pathogenesis of fibrosis involves a complex, self-reinforcing interplay of biochemical signals, including TGF-β and PDGFβ, biomechanical cues such as matrix stiffening and viscoelastic remodeling, and multicellular crosstalk among hepatocytes, HSCs, immune cells, and sinusoidal endothelial cells. Despite growing mechanistic understanding of fibrotic progression and regression, the development of effective antifibrotic therapeutics has been significantly hampered by the limited translational fidelity of existing experimental models. Here, we review the current landscape of liver fibrosis models, spanning conventional two-dimensional cell culture, organ-on-a-chip platforms, organoids, and biomaterial-based systems, with a focus on HSC biology. We critically evaluate the capacity of each platform to decouple and interrogate the biochemical, biophysical, and cell-to-cell signals that govern HSC activation, ECM deposition, and fibrotic remodeling. We highlight advances in tunable hydrogel systems and decellularized ECM scaffolds that enable precise control of matrix mechanics and composition, as well as the emergence of iPSC-derived HSCs as a scalable and phenotypically relevant cell source. title: Functional involvement of AMPK in Lumpy skin disease virus replication and associated cellular stress responses.
abstract: Lumpy skin disease virus (LSDV) infection induces extensive cellular stress responses and metabolic reprogramming in host cells. However, the regulatory mechanisms linking these changes to viral replication remain unclear. In this study, MAC-T cells were used as an in vitro infection model to investigate LSDV-induced cellular stress responses and their impact on viral replication. Transcriptomic analysis revealed that LSDV infection activated pathways associated with energy stress, oxidative stress, and endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress, suggesting disruption of cellular energy homeostasis and redox balance. Transmission electron microscopy further demonstrated mitochondrial structural damage in infected cells. Subsequent analyses showed that the ATP/AMP ratio and lactate metabolism decreased during infection, accompanied by elevated mitochondrial calcium levels and excessive reactive oxygen species accumulation. Mechanistically, LSDV infection activated the PERK-eIF2α-ATF4-CHOP and IRE1α-JNK-BECN1 pathways, indicating induction of ER stress-related signaling. Given the role of AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) as a central metabolic stress sensor, we further examined its function during LSDV infection. LSDV infection enhanced AMPK activation, as evidenced by increased phosphorylation of Thr172. title: Direct infusion intact mass spectrometry for rapid and sensitive characterization of antibody therapeutics in complex matrices.
abstract: Native intact mass spectrometry (MS) is essential for resolving the structural heterogeneity of complex biotherapeutics. Traditionally, intact MS combines online chromatography (e.g. ion-exchange chromatography or size-exclusion chromatography). Here, we report an MS-centric, column-free direct infusion MS workflow that combines high-throughput off-line 96-well affinity purification with rapid and sensitive direct infusion MS. This approach achieves a sampling rate of ~1 min/sample with minimal sample consumption ( 2 ≥ 0.99) in the 1.953-500 µg/mL range, enabling relative quantitation and relative quality ranking across samples based on the deconvoluted MS signal. The utility of this direct infusion MS workflow is demonstrated through two case studies: 1) analysis of antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) stability and biotransformation in mouse serum, where direct infusion MS successfully tracked changes in drug-load distribution and average drug-to-antibody ratio; and 2) sensitive, high-throughput MS screening during early-stage bispecific antibody clone development. The workflow allows early detection of high-quality bsAb clones, providing results that show potential as an early indicator of drug quality in expanded fed-batch cultures. The serum stability study illustrates how this direct infusion MS workflow - despite being column free - can reveal critical product changes in highly complex sample matrices using a robust, rapid, and sensitive workflow.
